threads.title: Making attention fast: from tiling to sparse and latent attention
threads.dek: Exact attention got fast by respecting GPU memory, the KV cache got small by sharing and compressing keys, and long context got cheap by learning which tokens to read at all.

sections.heading: Why attention is the expensive part
sections.md:
Self-attention, from Vaswani et al.'s 2017 Transformer, compares every query with every key. For a sequence of length $N$ the score matrix $S = QK^\top/\sqrt{d}$ is $N \times N$, so compute grows as $N^2$. A naive GPU kernel also writes $S$ and the softmax output $P$ to HBM (the GPU's large but slow off-chip memory) and reads them back. At $N = 8192$ in FP16 that is 128 MiB per head per matrix, for one layer.

During generation a different cost dominates. Each new token must read the **KV cache**, the stored keys and values of every earlier token, in every layer and head. Decoding is therefore limited by memory bandwidth, not arithmetic, and the cache size decides how many requests fit on a GPU. The NSA paper cites estimates that attention accounts for 70 to 80% of latency when decoding with a 64k-token context.

So there are really three problems, and this thread follows a separate line of work for each:

1. **Moving bytes during training and prefill.** Solved without approximation by IO-aware kernels (the FlashAttention line).
2. **The size of the KV cache.** Attacked by storing fewer or smaller keys and values (multi-query, grouped-query and multi-head latent attention).
3. **Reading the whole past for every token.** Attacked by sparse attention that is trained to read only what matters (NSA, DeepSeek Sparse Attention and their successors).

Linear attention and state space models, which drop the $N^2$ structure entirely, are a fourth route covered in the beyond-attention thread.

sections.heading: Exact but IO-aware: online softmax becomes FlashAttention
sections.md:
Early efficiency work changed the math. Child et al.'s Sparse Transformer (OpenAI, 2019) restricted each query to fixed strided patterns to get $O(N\sqrt{N})$ cost. Many later approximations cut FLOPs too, but the FlashAttention paper observed that they often did not deliver wall-clock speedups, because the real bottleneck was memory traffic.

The key enabler was older. In 2018 Milakov and Gimelshein (NVIDIA) showed that a softmax can be computed in one pass with a **running max and running sum**: when a larger value appears, rescale what you have so far. Rabe and Staats (Google, 2021) used blockwise processing to show self-attention does not need $O(n^2)$ memory.

**FlashAttention** (Dao, Fu, Ermon, Rudra and Re, 2022) turned this into a kernel. It tiles $Q$, $K$ and $V$ into blocks that fit in on-chip SRAM, keeps a running max $m$, sum $l$ and unnormalized output per query row, and never writes $S$ or $P$ to HBM. The backward pass recomputes them instead of storing them. The result is exact attention with linear memory and, per the paper, 2 to 4x speedups over standard implementations. The paper explicitly credits the softmax decomposition to Milakov and Gimelshein and compares itself with Rabe and Staats.

Each later version chased the bottleneck the next GPU exposed:

- **FlashAttention-2** (Dao, 2023) fixed work partitioning: it parallelizes over query blocks, splits work across warps without shared-memory exchanges, and divides by $l$ once at the end. The paper notes FlashAttention reached only 25 to 40% of peak FLOPs.
- **FlashAttention-3** (Shah et al., 2024) used Hopper's asynchronous tensor cores and TMA copy engine with producer and consumer warps, overlapped softmax with matmuls, and added accurate FP8 via block quantization and incoherent processing. The authors report 1.5 to 2.0x over FlashAttention-2 on H100.
- **FlashAttention-4** (Zadouri et al., 2026) targets Blackwell, where tensor cores doubled but the exponential unit and shared memory did not. It emulates part of $e^x$ with a polynomial on the FMA units and skips rescaling unless the max jumps by more than a threshold.

sections.heading: Shrinking the cache: from sharing heads to a learned latent
sections.md:
FlashAttention made the math fast, but decoding still reads the whole KV cache. With $n_h$ heads of size $d_h$ over $l$ layers, standard multi-head attention stores $2 n_h d_h l$ numbers per token.

**Multi-query attention** (MQA, Shazeer, 2019) lets all query heads share one key head and one value head, cutting the cache by $n_h$ times at some quality cost. **Grouped-query attention** (GQA, Ainslie et al., Google, 2023) interpolates: query heads are split into groups that each share a KV head. The GQA paper reports quality close to multi-head attention at speed comparable to MQA, and showed existing checkpoints can be uptrained to it with 5% of the original pretraining compute.

**Multi-head latent attention** (MLA), introduced in DeepSeek-V2 (2024), took a different route. Instead of sharing keys, it projects each token into one small latent vector $c_t$ (512 numbers in DeepSeek-V2 and V3) and derives every head's key and value from it with learned up-projections. Only the latent is cached. Because matrix products are associative, the key up-projection can be folded into the query at decode time, so the kernel attends directly over latents. Every head reads the same cached rows, which makes decode MQA-shaped in memory traffic while each head still sees its own keys.

Position encoding complicated this. RoPE rotates keys by position, which would sit between the query and the up-projection and block the folding. MLA's **decoupled RoPE** keeps a separate 64-wide rotated key shared by all heads, so the cache is $512 + 64 = 576$ elements per token per layer. In DeepSeek-V2's own ablations MLA scored better than MHA while caching far less, and its 7B-scale ablation found GQA and MQA below MHA on MMLU.

sections.heading: Sparse attention that is trained, not bolted on
sections.md:
Smaller caches still have to be read in full. Sparse methods try to read only the keys that matter. Many earlier methods (KV eviction, per-query block selection, hashing) were applied to already trained dense models. The **Native Sparse Attention** paper (Yuan et al., DeepSeek-AI and Peking University, 2025) argued they rarely delivered real speedups: some sped up only decode or only prefill, per-head selection broke GQA's shared cache, and the model never learned to work with the sparsity.

NSA is trained with sparsity from scratch. Each query attends through three branches mixed by learned gates: **compressed** summaries of blocks of past tokens, a **selected** set of full-resolution blocks (top-$n$ blocks scored by reusing the compressed branch's attention, shared across a GQA group), and a **sliding window** of recent tokens. A custom Triton kernel loads each selected block once for the whole group. On 8 A100s the authors report forward speedups of up to 9.0x over FlashAttention-2 at 64k tokens, and a 27B MoE model that matched or beat its full-attention twin on their benchmarks.

**DeepSeek Sparse Attention** (DSA), in DeepSeek-V3.2 (2025), simplified this. A cheap FP8 **lightning indexer** scores every past token, and the main attention reads only the top 2048. DSA is built on MLA in its MQA mode, citing NSA's point that each KV entry must be shared across queries for kernel efficiency. It was added to an existing dense checkpoint by continued training: the indexer first learns to imitate dense attention scores, then everything trains sparsely.

Neither NSA nor DSA shrinks the stored cache; they cut what is read and computed per token. DSA's indexer is still quadratic over a sequence, just with a much smaller constant.

sections.heading: Where it is now: compression and sparsity stacked together
sections.md:
The newest systems combine the three ideas instead of choosing one.

**DeepSeek-V4** (April 2026) folds DSA into a hybrid of **Compressed Sparse Attention** (CSA), which compresses every $m$ tokens of KV into one entry and then applies DSA, with the lightning indexer now computed in FP4, to pick the top-$k$ compressed entries, and **Heavily Compressed Attention** (HCA), which compresses far more aggressively and attends densely over the result. A small sliding window covers recent tokens, KV is stored mostly in FP8, and both attention types are multi-query. The report states that at a 1M-token context V4-Pro needs 27% of the per-token inference FLOPs and 10% of the KV cache of DeepSeek-V3.2.

DSA itself spread beyond DeepSeek: Zhipu's **GLM-5** report (February 2026) says the model adopts DSA to cut training and inference cost while keeping long-context fidelity.

On the kernel side, **FlashAttention-4** (March 2026) shows the exact-attention line is far from finished. The authors report up to 1613 TFLOPs/s in BF16 on B200 (71% utilization), written entirely in the Python-embedded CuTe-DSL, and note that cuDNN has since adopted many of the same techniques.

A smaller, widely adopted change is **gated attention** (Qiu et al., Qwen, 2025): a head-specific sigmoid gate after attention. Across 30 variants of 15B MoE and 1.7B dense models, the authors found it consistently improved quality and stability and removed the "attention sink" where heads dump weight on the first token. The Qwen3-Next and Qwen3.5 model cards list gated attention for their full-attention layers.

sections.heading: How these pieces show up in a serving stack
sections.md:
In practice an inference engine mixes forms depending on the phase. vLLM's MLA implementation uses the absorbed, MQA-shaped path for decode, where memory traffic dominates, and up-projects latents into ordinary per-head keys and values for prefill, where compute dominates. DeepSeek's FlashMLA write-up estimates that with all 128 heads on one GPU the decode kernel is close to compute-bound, unusual for attention.

The cache trick also changes parallelism. GQA's KV heads can be split across GPUs, but MLA has effectively one KV head, so tensor parallelism over heads duplicates the whole latent cache on every GPU. vLLM documents this and offers context parallelism, sharding the cache along the sequence instead.

The lesson that runs through the whole thread: theoretical FLOP savings are not speedups. FlashAttention won by counting bytes, MLA by counting cache elements, and NSA and DSA by making every head in a group read the same contiguous memory.

lineage.title: Attention Is All You Need
lineage.contribution: Introduced the Transformer, built on scaled dot-product multi-head attention, whose cost grows quadratically with sequence length and whose decoding needs a per-token cache of keys and values.

lineage.title: Online normalizer calculation for softmax
lineage.contribution: Computed softmax in a single pass by keeping a running max and a running sum that is rescaled when the max grows, cutting memory accesses. This is the trick that later lets attention be computed block by block.

lineage.title: Generating Long Sequences with Sparse Transformers
lineage.contribution: Factorized attention into fixed sparse patterns with O(n sqrt n) cost, plus recomputation and custom kernels, an early demonstration that sequences tens of thousands of tokens long could be modeled.

lineage.title: Fast Transformer Decoding: One Write-Head is All You Need (multi-query attention)
lineage.contribution: Shared a single key head and value head across all query heads, shrinking the KV cache and the memory bandwidth of incremental decoding with minor quality loss.

lineage.title: Self-attention Does Not Need O(n^2) Memory
lineage.contribution: Showed attention can be computed in chunks with O(sqrt n) memory in a practical implementation, and how to differentiate it memory-efficiently, though runtime stayed close to standard attention.

lineage.title: FlashAttention: Fast and Memory-Efficient Exact Attention with IO-Awareness
lineage.contribution: Made exact attention IO-aware: tiles Q, K, V into on-chip SRAM, uses online softmax so the N by N matrices never reach HBM, and recomputes them in the backward pass. Reported 2 to 4x speedups with linear memory.

lineage.title: GQA: Training Generalized Multi-Query Transformer Models from Multi-Head Checkpoints
lineage.who: Ainslie, Lee-Thorp, de Jong et al. (Google Research)
lineage.contribution: Grouped query heads so each group shares one KV head, an intermediate between multi-head and multi-query attention, and showed how to uptrain existing checkpoints with 5% of pretraining compute.

lineage.title: FlashAttention-2: Faster Attention with Better Parallelism and Work Partitioning
lineage.contribution: Reduced non-matmul work, parallelized over query blocks and split work across warps without shared-memory exchange, lifting utilization well above the 25 to 40% of peak the first version reached.

lineage.title: DeepSeek-V2 (introduces multi-head latent attention, MLA)
lineage.contribution: Cached one learned low-rank latent per token instead of per-head keys and values, folded the up-projections into the query at decode time, and added a decoupled shared RoPE key. Motivated as a better trade-off than MQA and GQA.

lineage.title: FlashAttention-3: Fast and Accurate Attention with Asynchrony and Low-precision
lineage.who: Shah, Bikshandi, Zhang, Thakkar, Ramani, Dao
lineage.contribution: Redesigned the kernel for Hopper: warp-specialized producers and consumers, ping-pong overlap of softmax with matmuls, and FP8 with block quantization and incoherent processing. Reported 1.5 to 2.0x over FlashAttention-2 on H100.

lineage.title: Native Sparse Attention: Hardware-Aligned and Natively Trainable Sparse Attention
lineage.who: Yuan, Gao, Dai et al. (DeepSeek-AI, Peking University)
lineage.contribution: Trained sparse attention from scratch with compressed, selected and sliding-window branches, sharing block selection across a GQA group so a custom kernel loads each block once. Reported large training and decoding speedups at 64k tokens.

lineage.title: DeepSeek-V3.2 (DeepSeek Sparse Attention, DSA)
lineage.contribution: A lightweight FP8 lightning indexer scores past tokens and the main MLA attention, run in MQA mode, reads only the top 2048. Added to a dense checkpoint by continued training. First shipped in DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp.

lineage.title: FlashAttention-4: Algorithm and Kernel Pipelining Co-Design for Asymmetric Hardware Scaling
lineage.who: Zadouri, Hoehnerbach, Shah, Liu, Thakkar, Dao
lineage.contribution: Targets Blackwell, where tensor cores outpaced the exponential unit and shared memory: software-emulated exponentials, conditional rescaling, tensor-memory pipelines and 2-CTA MMA in the backward pass, written in CuTe-DSL.

frontier.title: DeepSeek-V4: Compressed Sparse Attention plus Heavily Compressed Attention
frontier.note: Interleaves CSA (KV compressed every m tokens, top-k selection by an FP4 lightning indexer) with HCA (much heavier compression, dense attention), plus a sliding window. The report states V4-Pro needs 27% of the per-token FLOPs and 10% of the KV cache of DeepSeek-V3.2 at 1M tokens.

frontier.title: FlashAttention-4 for Blackwell GPUs
frontier.who: Zadouri, Hoehnerbach, Shah, Liu, Thakkar, Dao
frontier.note: Shows exact attention still has headroom when hardware scales unevenly. The paper reports up to 1613 TFLOPs/s BF16 on B200 (71% utilization) and 1.1 to 1.3x over cuDNN 9.13; the authors note newer cuDNN versions adopted many of the same techniques.

frontier.title: GLM-5 adopts DeepSeek Sparse Attention
frontier.note: The GLM-5 report states the model adopts DSA to cut training and inference cost while keeping long-context fidelity, an early sign that a trained sparse attention design is spreading beyond the lab that created it.

frontier.title: DeepSeek-V3.2 paper describes DSA in full
frontier.note: Documents the lightning indexer, its two-stage training (dense warm-up to imitate attention scores, then sparse training) and why DSA sits on MLA's MQA mode. DSA was the only architectural change from V3.1-Terminus, which makes it a clean case study.

frontier.title: Gated Attention for Large Language Models
frontier.who: Qiu, Wang, Zheng et al. (Qwen team, Alibaba)
frontier.note: A head-specific sigmoid gate after attention consistently improved quality and training stability across 30 variants of 15B MoE and 1.7B dense models, and mitigated the attention sink. The same team's Qwen3-Next and Qwen3.5 model cards list "Gated Attention" as their full-attention layer type.

open: How far can KV compression go before long-range retrieval breaks? DeepSeek-V4 compresses aggressively, but independent long-context evaluations of such designs are still scarce.
Can a learned indexer avoid becoming the new quadratic bottleneck at multi-million-token contexts, given that it still scores every past token or block?
Sparse and compressed attention rarely shrink what must be stored and add kernel complexity. Which designs will standard inference engines support well enough to become defaults?
Each GPU generation moved the bottleneck (HBM, then warp scheduling, then the exponential unit). Will future kernels need algorithm changes, not just scheduling, to keep attention near peak?
Retrofitting works (GQA uptraining, MHA2MLA, DSA continued training), but how much quality is lost versus training the efficient form from scratch at frontier scale?

connects.why: Linear attention and state space models remove the quadratic cost entirely; hybrids keep a few full-attention layers that still need the kernels and cache tricks here.
DeepSeek-V2, V3, V3.2 and V4 pair MLA and sparse attention with fine-grained MoE; serving them means solving cache and expert parallelism together.
Test-time-training layers and Titans frame attention as short-term memory and add learned long-term memory, another answer to the growing KV cache.

threads.title: Beyond attention: state space models, linear attention and hybrids
threads.dek: Recurrent layers with a fixed-size memory came back as linear attention, Mamba and Gated DeltaNet. They did not replace attention, but most new long-context models now mix them with a few attention layers.

sections.heading: The price of remembering everything
sections.md:
A softmax attention layer keeps every past token's key and value in a **KV cache** and compares each new token against all of them. That makes lookup exact, but memory grows linearly with context and total compute grows quadratically. AI21's Jamba paper gives a concrete number: at 256K tokens, Llama-2 7B (32 layers, 32 KV heads of size 128, 16-bit) needs 128 GiB of KV cache for a single sequence.

An RNN does the opposite. It folds each token into a **fixed-size state**, so each new token costs the same no matter how long the context is. Classic RNNs lost to Transformers for two reasons: training is sequential over time, which wastes GPUs, and a small vector state forgets.

Everything in this thread is an attempt to get both properties: a recurrent, constant-memory form for generation and a parallel, matmul-friendly form for training. Two research communities arrived at nearly the same answer from different starting points. One began from attention and removed the softmax (**linear attention**). The other began from control theory and discretized continuous systems (**state space models**, SSMs). By 2024 they were shown to be two views of one family, and by 2025 the practical question had become how to mix them with attention.

sections.heading: Two roads to a recurrent Transformer
sections.md:
**Linear attention.** Katharopoulos et al. (Idiap and EPFL, 2020) wrote attention with a similarity $\phi(q)^\top\phi(k)$ instead of $\exp(q^\top k)$. Matrix products can then be regrouped so the $N \times N$ matrix never forms: the past is summarized by a matrix state $S_t = S_{t-1} + v_t k_t^\top$, read as $o_t = S_t q_t$. The paper's title says it: Transformers are RNNs. Schlag, Irie and Schmidhuber (IDSIA, 2021) then showed this state is a **fast weight memory** that stores key-value pairs by adding outer products. They identified its weakness: it can only add, never overwrite, and it holds roughly $d_k$ clean associations before stored values blur together. They proposed the **delta rule** fix: read what the memory currently returns for $k_t$ and replace it.

**State space models.** Gu and colleagues at Stanford started from HiPPO (2020), a principled way to compress a signal's history online into polynomial coefficients. **S4** (Gu, Goel and Re, 2021) made the resulting linear state space layer efficient to train as a long convolution and set strong results on long-range benchmarks. But S4's dynamics were fixed per layer, independent of the input, which hurt on language.

**Mamba** (Gu and Dao, 2023) made the SSM parameters functions of the current token, so the layer can choose what to keep and what to forget. That broke the convolution trick, so the authors wrote a hardware-aware parallel scan. They reported 5x higher inference throughput than Transformers and strong language modeling at small and medium scale. In parallel, **Gated Linear Attention** (Yang et al., 2023) added data-dependent decay gates to linear attention with an IO-aware chunkwise kernel.

sections.heading: The roads merge: Mamba-2, DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet
sections.md:
**Mamba-2** (Dao and Gu, 2024) proved the connection formally. Its **state space duality** shows a selective SSM with scalar decay per head is the same function as masked linear attention whose mask multiplies decays between positions. That gives two ways to compute one layer: a recurrent form for decoding and a quadratic, matmul-friendly form used inside chunks for training. The paper reports its kernel is 2 to 8x faster than Mamba's scan.

The remaining weakness was recall. A decay gate forgets everything at the same rate, so it cannot remove one stale fact while keeping others. The delta rule can, but it was strictly sequential to train. Yang et al. (2024) found a chunkwise parallel algorithm for **DeltaNet** using a compact representation of products of Householder-like matrices, trained a 1.3B model on 100B tokens, and reported better perplexity and zero-shot results than Mamba and GLA.

**Gated DeltaNet** (Yang, Kautz and Hatamizadeh, NVIDIA, 2024) combined the two: decay the whole state by a data-dependent $\alpha_t$, then apply a targeted delta-rule write. In the paper's words, gating enables rapid erasure while the delta rule enables targeted updates. In an online-learning view, the state is a set of fast weights trained by one gradient step per token, with $\beta_t$ as the learning rate and $\alpha_t$ as weight decay. The same view underlies the memory-and-depth thread's test-time training layers.

Even so, a fixed state compresses. At equal training data, NVIDIA's 8B comparison (Waleffe et al., 2024) found pure Mamba models matched or beat Transformers on many tasks but lagged on copying, in-context learning such as 5-shot MMLU, and long-context reasoning.

sections.heading: Why hybrids won the first round
sections.md:
If the state is good at cheap, smooth mixing and attention is good at exact lookup, use both. **Jamba** (AI21, 2024) interleaved one attention layer for every seven Mamba layers, with MoE in every other layer. Its authors reported that a pure Mamba model failed to follow few-shot output formats, and that adding attention fixed it, with induction-like heads appearing in the attention layers. With only 4 attention layers, Jamba's KV cache at 256K tokens was 4 GiB versus 32 GiB for Mixtral.

The same NVIDIA study that exposed Mamba's recall gap built **Mamba-2-Hybrid**: 43% Mamba-2, 7% attention and 50% MLP layers. At 8B and 3.5T tokens it beat the matched Transformer on the evaluated tasks and was predicted to generate up to 8x faster at long context. **Nemotron-H** (NVIDIA, 2025) scaled that recipe to 8B and 56B models and reported accuracy on par with similar open Transformers at up to 3x the inference speed.

Linear attention followed. **Qwen3-Next** (Alibaba, September 2025) shipped 48 layers as 12 repeats of three Gated DeltaNet layers and one gated full-attention layer, each followed by MoE. **Kimi Linear** (Moonshot, October 2025) introduced Kimi Delta Attention, a Gated DeltaNet with finer per-channel gating, mixed with MLA layers. Under an identical training recipe the authors report it beat full MLA while cutting KV cache by up to 75% and reaching up to 6x decoding throughput at 1M tokens.

The common design rule from these ablations: keep a small fraction of layers as global attention, spread them out, and let recurrent layers do the rest.

sections.heading: Where it is now: production hybrids, Mamba-3, and a dissent
sections.md:
Hybrids are now shipping at frontier scale, and the newest releases keep the pattern: Moonshot's **Kimi K3** (July 2026, 2.8T parameters) mixes 69 Kimi Delta Attention layers with 24 gated MLA layers, and **Qwen3.8** (August 2026, 2.4T) repeats Qwen3.5's 3:1 layout. **Qwen3.5** (February 2026) carried the Qwen3-Next layout to a 397B-parameter MoE: per its model card, 60 layers as 15 blocks of three Gated DeltaNet layers and one gated attention layer, with a native 262,144-token context. NVIDIA's **Nemotron 3** family (white paper, December 2025) uses a hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE design with contexts up to 1M tokens, and the **Nemotron 3 Ultra** report (June 2026) describes a 550B-total, 55B-active hybrid that the authors say reaches up to about 6x higher inference throughput than comparable open models at on-par accuracy.

On the recurrent side, **Mamba-3** (Lahoti et al., with Dao and Gu, March 2026) designs for inference first. It adds an SSM-derived discretization, complex-valued state transitions for state tracking, and a multi-input, multi-output form that does more work per state update without adding decode latency. At 1.5B scale the authors report 0.6 points better average downstream accuracy than Gated DeltaNet (1.8 with MIMO), and Mamba-2-level perplexity with half the state size.

Not everyone went hybrid. MiniMax's M1 used a Lightning (linear) attention hybrid, but the M2 pretraining lead wrote in October 2025 that M2 returned to full attention. The post reports that hybrids matched full attention on standard benchmarks but showed clear deficits in complex multi-hop reasoning at larger scale, that linear attention is far more sensitive to numerical precision, and that inference infrastructure (prefix caching, speculative decoding) is less mature. DeepSeek, meanwhile, took the compressed and sparse attention route described in the efficient-attention thread. The honest summary is that hybrids won the first round on efficiency, and the evaluation of their weaknesses on long agentic tasks is still going on.

lineage.title: Transformers are RNNs: Fast Autoregressive Transformers with Linear Attention
lineage.contribution: Replaced softmax with a kernel feature map so attention can be regrouped into a running matrix state: linear time, constant memory per generated token, and an explicit RNN view of the Transformer.

lineage.title: HiPPO: Recurrent Memory with Optimal Polynomial Projections
lineage.contribution: A framework for compressing a signal's whole history online by projecting it onto polynomial bases, giving principled state matrices for recurrent memory that later SSMs initialize from.

lineage.title: Linear Transformers Are Secretly Fast Weight Programmers
lineage.contribution: Showed linear attention equals a fast weight memory written by outer products, derived its capacity limit, and replaced the additive write with a delta-rule update that can correct stored associations.

lineage.title: Efficiently Modeling Long Sequences with Structured State Spaces (S4)
lineage.contribution: Reparameterized the HiPPO state space model so it can be computed efficiently as a long convolution, making SSMs a practical sequence layer with strong long-range results.

lineage.title: Mamba: Linear-Time Sequence Modeling with Selective State Spaces
lineage.contribution: Made SSM parameters depend on the input so the layer selects what to remember, with a hardware-aware parallel scan. Reported 5x Transformer inference throughput and strong language modeling at small and medium scale.

lineage.title: Gated Linear Attention Transformers with Hardware-Efficient Training
lineage.who: Yang, Wang, Shen, Panda, Kim (MIT, MIT-IBM)
lineage.contribution: Added data-dependent decay gates to linear attention and an IO-aware chunkwise kernel (FlashLinearAttention) faster than FlashAttention-2 as a standalone layer even at 1K tokens.

lineage.title: Jamba: A Hybrid Transformer-Mamba Language Model
lineage.who: Lieber, Lenz, Bata et al. (AI21 Labs)
lineage.contribution: Interleaved 1 attention layer per 7 Mamba layers with MoE, showing attention restores in-context learning that pure Mamba lacked, with an 8x smaller KV cache than a comparable Transformer at 256K tokens.

lineage.title: Transformers are SSMs: Structured State Space Duality (Mamba-2)
lineage.contribution: Proved selective SSMs with scalar decay are a form of masked linear attention, giving a chunked matmul training algorithm. The resulting Mamba-2 layer is 2 to 8x faster than Mamba's scan.

lineage.title: Parallelizing Linear Transformers with the Delta Rule over Sequence Length
lineage.contribution: A chunkwise parallel algorithm for DeltaNet using a compact form of Householder products, scaling it to a 1.3B model on 100B tokens that beat Mamba and GLA baselines.

lineage.title: An Empirical Study of Mamba-based Language Models
lineage.who: Waleffe, Byeon, Riach et al. (NVIDIA, with Dao and Gu)
lineage.contribution: Matched 8B Mamba, Mamba-2 and Transformer models on 3.5T tokens: pure SSMs lagged on copying and in-context learning, while a hybrid with 7% attention beat the Transformer on the evaluated tasks.

lineage.title: Gated Delta Networks: Improving Mamba2 with Delta Rule
lineage.contribution: Combined Mamba-2 style decay gating (fast erasure) with the delta rule (targeted overwrite) in one parallel-trainable layer, plus hybrids with sliding-window attention. Reported gains over Mamba2 and DeltaNet.

lineage.title: Nemotron-H: A Family of Accurate and Efficient Hybrid Mamba-Transformer Models
lineage.contribution: Scaled the Mamba-2 hybrid recipe to 8B and 56B models that the authors report match similar open Transformers in accuracy at up to 3x faster inference.

lineage.title: Qwen3-Next-80B-A3B
lineage.contribution: An open MoE model whose 48 layers repeat three Gated DeltaNet layers and one gated full-attention layer, bringing linear-attention hybrids into a widely used model family.

lineage.title: Kimi Linear: An Expressive, Efficient Attention Architecture
lineage.contribution: Kimi Delta Attention extends Gated DeltaNet with finer-grained gating; hybridized with MLA it is reported to beat full MLA under the same recipe, with up to 75% less KV cache and 6x decoding throughput at 1M tokens.

frontier.title: Qwen3.8 keeps the 3:1 Gated DeltaNet hybrid at 2.4T
frontier.note: The 2.4T-total, 95B-active model card lists 92 layers as 23 x (3 Gated DeltaNet + 1 gated attention), each followed by MoE (512 experts, 10 routed + 1 shared), with a native 262,144-token context: the Qwen3-Next and Qwen3.5 layout carried to trillion-parameter scale.

frontier.title: Kimi K3 scales Kimi Delta Attention to 2.8T parameters
frontier.note: A 2.8T-total, 104B-active MoE whose model card lists 93 layers: 69 Kimi Delta Attention layers and 24 gated MLA layers, with a 1M-token context. It takes the Kimi Linear hybrid from a 48B research model to a released frontier-scale model, about three linear layers per attention layer.

frontier.title: Nemotron 3 Ultra: a 550B hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE
frontier.note: A 550B-total, 55B-active hybrid Mamba-attention MoE pretrained on 20T tokens and extended to 1M context. The authors report up to about 6x higher inference throughput than comparable public models at on-par accuracy, showing SSM hybrids at frontier scale.

frontier.title: Mamba-3: Improved Sequence Modeling using State Space Principles
frontier.who: Lahoti, Li, Chen, Wang, Bick, Kolter, Dao, Gu
frontier.note: Inference-first redesign: SSM-derived discretization, complex-valued transitions for state tracking, and a MIMO form. At 1.5B the authors report +0.6 points over Gated DeltaNet (+1.8 with MIMO) and Mamba-2 perplexity at half the state size.

frontier.title: Qwen3.5 scales the Gated DeltaNet hybrid to 397B
frontier.note: The model card lists 60 layers as 15 x (3 Gated DeltaNet + 1 gated attention), each followed by MoE (512 experts), 17B active parameters and a native 262,144-token context, so three quarters of layers keep no KV cache.

frontier.title: NVIDIA Nemotron 3 family (Nano, Super, Ultra)
frontier.note: White paper for a family built on a mixture-of-experts hybrid Mamba-Transformer design with contexts up to 1M tokens, adding LatentMoE and NVFP4 training for the larger models.

frontier.title: Kimi Linear claims a hybrid beats full attention
frontier.note: A 48B-total, 3B-active model mixing Kimi Delta Attention with MLA. The authors report it outperforms full MLA under an identical recipe on short, long and RL tasks; independent replication at larger scale is still limited.

frontier.title: Why did MiniMax M2 end up as a full attention model?
frontier.note: A rare negative report: after M1's linear-attention hybrid, M2 went back to full attention. The post cites deficits in complex multi-hop reasoning at scale, numerical precision sensitivity, and immature infrastructure for linear models.

open: Do hybrids keep their benchmark parity on long, multi-hop agentic tasks? MiniMax reports deficits at scale while Moonshot reports gains; controlled public comparisons are still rare.
What is the right ratio and placement of attention layers at frontier scale? Published ablations (about 1 in 4 to 1 in 8) were mostly run on models far smaller than the ones that ship.
Can richer state updates (complex transitions, MIMO, delta rules) close the exact-recall gap so fewer attention layers are needed, or is some attention always required?
How should a fixed recurrent state be stored in low precision, cached across shared prefixes, and rolled back for speculative decoding?
Will compressed and sparse attention (as in DeepSeek-V4) or recurrent hybrids become the default route to million-token contexts?

connects.why: The attention layers inside every hybrid still rely on FlashAttention-style kernels, and sparse or compressed attention is the competing route to long context.
Gated DeltaNet's state is fast weights trained by one gradient step per token; test-time training layers and Titans generalize that idea to deeper learned memories.
Jamba, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, Kimi Linear and Nemotron 3 all pair recurrent hybrids with MoE feed-forward layers.

threads.title: Mixture of experts: sparse models that scale
threads.dek: Mixture-of-experts layers let a model store far more parameters than any one token uses. Making that work took better routers, load balancing that does not fight the loss, and serving systems built around expert traffic.

sections.heading: Parameters are cheap to store, expensive to use
sections.md:
In a dense Transformer every token passes through every weight of every feed-forward network (FFN). Doubling the parameters doubles the compute per token. That couples two things you might want to scale separately: how much the model can store, and how much work each token costs.

A **mixture-of-experts** (MoE) layer replaces one FFN with $N$ **experts**, each an ordinary FFN, plus a small **router** that scores the experts for each token and runs only the top $K$. Parameters grow with $N$, compute grows with $K$. DeepSeek-V3, for example, has 671B total parameters but activates 37B per token, and its report states the full training took 2.788M H800 GPU hours.

The idea is simple; making it work is not. Four problems recur through this thread:

1. **Routing collapse.** The router learns to favor a few experts, which then train faster and get picked even more, while the rest stay untrained.
2. **Load imbalance.** With experts spread across GPUs (**expert parallelism**), the busiest GPU sets the speed of every step.
3. **Specialization.** With few large experts, each one has to hold many unrelated kinds of knowledge.
4. **Communication.** Every MoE layer sends tokens to the GPUs that hold their experts and back again, an all-to-all exchange that can dominate the step time.

The history of MoE is mostly a history of answers to these four problems.

sections.heading: From sparsely gated layers to Switch: making sparsity trainable
sections.md:
**Sparsely-gated MoE** (Shazeer, Mirhoseini, Maziarz, Davis, Le, Hinton and Dean, Google, 2017) made conditional computation work at scale. A trainable gating network picks a sparse combination of up to thousands of experts per example, inserted between LSTM layers for language modeling and translation. The authors reported over 1000x gains in model capacity with only minor losses in computational efficiency. Two ideas from the paper stayed: add noise to the gate scores to encourage exploration, and add an **auxiliary balance loss** so experts receive similar shares of the batch.

**GShard** (Lepikhin et al., Google, 2020) brought MoE into the Transformer, replacing every other FFN with a top-2 MoE layer, and built XLA compiler support for sharding experts across devices. It trained a 600B-parameter translation model on 2048 TPU v3 chips in 4 days. To keep tensor shapes static it gave each expert a fixed **capacity**; tokens beyond it are dropped and pass through only the residual connection.

**Switch Transformer** (Fedus, Zoph and Shazeer, 2021) simplified routing to a single expert per token ($K = 1$), which halves expert compute and communication. With a simplified balance loss, selective float32 precision in the router and smaller initialization, the authors trained sparse models stably in bfloat16 and reported up to 7x pretraining speedups over T5 at equal compute. **ST-MoE** (Zoph et al., 2022) then focused on stability and fine-tuning, adding the **router z-loss**, which penalizes large router logits, and scaled to a 269B sparse model with the cost of a 32B dense one.

An alternative was **Expert Choice** routing (Zhou et al., Google, 2022): experts pick their top tokens instead of tokens picking experts, which gives perfect balance. In a causal language model, though, letting later tokens influence earlier tokens' routing can leak future information, a problem DeepSeek's loss-free balancing paper later quantified.

sections.heading: Many small experts, shared experts and dropless kernels
sections.md:
Two systems papers changed what was practical. **DeepSpeed-MoE** (Rajbhandari et al., Microsoft, 2022) built an end-to-end training and inference stack and proposed **Residual-MoE**, where a fixed dense MLP runs for every token alongside the routed expert. **MegaBlocks** (Gale, Narayanan, Young and Zaharia, 2022) recast MoE computation as block-sparse matrix multiplies, so experts can receive any number of tokens: no capacity limit, no dropped tokens and no padding.

**Mixtral 8x7B** (Mistral AI, January 2024) made MoE mainstream in open weights: 8 experts per layer, top-2, 47B total and 13B active, with inference through vLLM's integration of MegaBlocks kernels.

The same month, **DeepSeekMoE** (Dai et al., DeepSeek-AI, 2024) argued that 8 or 16 large experts cause *knowledge hybridity* (each expert must hold unrelated knowledge) and *redundancy* (every expert relearns common knowledge). Its fixes:

- **Fine-grained experts.** Split each expert into $m$ narrower ones and activate $m$ times more. Compute stays the same, but the number of possible expert combinations explodes, from 120 for top-2 of 16 to over 4 billion for top-8 of 64.
- **Shared experts.** A few experts every token always uses, holding common knowledge. The paper credits DeepSpeed-MoE for the prototype.

The authors report DeepSeekMoE 2B matched GShard 2.9B, which had 1.5x the expert parameters and compute. Independently, Krajewski et al. (University of Warsaw and IDEAS NCBR, 2024) fit scaling laws with **granularity** as a variable and found that making experts the same size as the dense FFN is not optimal at almost any compute budget.

sections.heading: Balancing without a balance loss
sections.md:
The auxiliary balance loss has a cost. Its gradient pushes the router toward even load, not toward predicting the next token. **Loss-Free Balancing** (Wang, Gao, Zhao, Sun and Dai, DeepSeek-AI, 2024) measured the dilemma: a small loss weight let routing collapse, while a large one balanced load but noticeably hurt perplexity. They call these *interference gradients*.

The fix is a per-expert bias $b_i$ added to the router scores only when choosing the top-$K$ experts. The gate weights still use the original scores. After each step the bias moves by a fixed amount: up for experts that were underloaded, down for overloaded ones. No gradient flows through it, so the language-modeling objective is untouched. Updating from the previous batch, rather than balancing the current one exactly, avoids the future-token leakage of Expert Choice.

**DeepSeek-V3** (December 2024) combined all of it: 256 fine-grained routed experts plus 1 shared expert per MoE layer, 8 routed experts per token, sigmoid router scores, bias-based balancing, and only a tiny sequence-wise balance loss as a safety net. To bound communication, each token may go to experts on at most 4 nodes. The report states no tokens were dropped during training.

Balancing over a whole batch, rather than within each sequence, also lets experts specialize by domain. The V3 report shows clearer domain-specific expert load in an auxiliary-loss-free model than with a sequence-wise loss.

sections.heading: Where it is now: more, smaller and cheaper experts
sections.md:
Recent open models keep raising **sparsity**, the ratio of total to active experts. **Kimi K2** (Moonshot, July 2025) uses 384 experts with 8 active and 1 shared, about 1T total and 32B active. Its report describes a sparsity scaling law: at fixed active parameters, more total experts consistently lowered loss, and at a validation loss of 1.5 sparsity 48 needed 1.69x fewer FLOPs than sparsity 8. The authors chose 48 to balance quality against infrastructure cost. **Qwen3.5** (February 2026) goes further: its model card lists 512 experts with 10 routed and 1 shared active, 397B total and 17B active.

NVIDIA's **LatentMoE** (Nemotron 3, December 2025) attacks the byte cost directly. Tokens are projected into a smaller latent dimension before routing and expert computation, cutting expert weight loads and all-to-all traffic by the ratio $d/\ell$ (typically about 4x). The saving is spent on proportionally more experts and more active experts at roughly constant inference cost. Moonshot's **Kimi K3** (July 2026) uses a LatentMoE design with 896 experts, 16 of them active per token, at 2.8T total and 104B active parameters.

**DeepSeek-V4** (April 2026) keeps fine-grained and shared experts and auxiliary-loss-free balancing, but changes the router's score function to $\sqrt{\mathrm{softplus}(\cdot)}$, removes the limit on how many nodes a token may route to, and replaces the dense FFN in the first few layers with MoE layers routed by a fixed hash of the token ID.

Serving has become its own discipline. SGLang's May 2025 deployment of DeepSeek on 96 H100s combined prefill-decode disaggregation, DeepSeek's DeepEP all-to-all library and its EPLB expert load balancer (which replicates hot experts). The authors report up to 5x the output throughput of a tensor-parallel baseline on the same hardware, and speedups from EPLB alone of 1.49x in prefill and 2.54x in decode.

open: How far does sparsity keep paying? Kimi K2 reports gains up to 48 and Qwen3.5 ships about 51 (512 routed, 10 active), but the infrastructure cost of very many small experts is still poorly quantified.
Do experts actually specialize in interpretable ways, or is specialization mostly a side effect of load balancing choices?
Can routing be made robust to domain shift at serving time, when one kind of traffic overloads a few experts, without replicating experts on the fly?
Is token-choice top-k routing the end state, or will learned per-token compute (variable numbers of experts, or skipping layers) win?
How should MoE models be fine-tuned and quantized when rarely used experts see little data?

connects.why: DeepSeek's MoE models pair experts with MLA and sparse attention; serving them means balancing KV cache and expert placement together.
Jamba, Qwen3-Next, Qwen3.5, Kimi Linear and Nemotron 3 combine MoE feed-forward layers with recurrent or hybrid sequence mixers.
MoE varies which parameters a token uses; looped and recurrent-depth models vary how much compute a token gets. Both decouple parameters from per-token FLOPs.

threads.title: Diffusion language models: generating text in parallel
threads.dek: Instead of writing one token at a time, a diffusion LM starts from a block of blanks and fills many in at once. Here is how masked diffusion went from a curiosity to 100B-parameter open models and commercial APIs.

sections.heading: One token per forward pass is the bottleneck
sections.md:
An autoregressive (AR) language model writes left to right: each new token needs a full forward pass through the network, conditioned on everything before it. At small batch sizes that pass is dominated by reading the weights from memory, so most of the GPU's arithmetic sits idle while the model emits a single token. Long answers, and especially long reasoning traces, are slow for this reason alone.

A **diffusion language model** changes the generation order. It starts from a sequence (or block) of placeholder tokens and repeatedly predicts all of them in parallel, keeping the predictions it is confident about and revisiting the rest. Each pass can finalize many tokens. Google's DiffusionGemma model card reports roughly 15 to 20 tokens per forward pass; NVIDIA reports that its Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion 8B model decodes 5.9 times more tokens per forward pass than Qwen3-8B.

The cost is that the model must learn to predict tokens whose neighbours are also unknown, and parallel guesses can disagree with each other. The research story is about making that trade worth it.

sections.heading: From image noise to masked tokens
sections.md:
Diffusion models began with Sohl-Dickstein and colleagues (2015): slowly destroy data with a fixed noising process, then train a network to reverse it step by step. That works naturally for continuous pixels, but text is a sequence of discrete symbols, so "add a little Gaussian noise" has no direct meaning.

Two routes followed. The **discrete** route replaced Gaussian noise with random token corruption. Hoogeboom et al. (2021) introduced *multinomial diffusion*, which resamples tokens toward a uniform distribution. Austin et al. (2021) generalized this as **D3PM**, where any transition matrix defines the corruption, including an *absorbing state*: each token is independently replaced by a special `[MASK]` token, and once masked it stays masked. The D3PM paper noted that this absorbing version connects diffusion to masked language models such as BERT (2018), which already learned to fill in masked words.

The **continuous** route, Diffusion-LM from Li et al. (2022), ran Gaussian diffusion over word embeddings and rounded back to tokens at the end. It enabled gradient-based control of syntax and other attributes, but rounding was fragile and likelihoods lagged far behind AR models.

Meanwhile MaskGIT (Chang et al., 2022) showed in images what parallel decoding could buy: a bidirectional transformer predicts every masked token at once, keeps the most confident ones, and remasks the rest. The paper reports up to 64x faster decoding than raster-order AR generation. That confidence-based unmasking loop is essentially the sampler most text diffusion models still use.

sections.heading: Closing the likelihood gap, 2023 to 2024
sections.md:
For years discrete diffusion trailed AR models badly on perplexity. Lou, Meng and Ermon's **SEDD** (2023) attacked the training objective: they proposed *score entropy*, a discrete analogue of score matching that learns ratios between the probabilities of neighbouring sequences. The authors report 25 to 75 percent lower perplexity than earlier diffusion LMs and results competitive with GPT-2, plus a direct compute and quality dial (similar quality with 32x fewer network evaluations).

In mid-2024 three groups independently showed the absorbing (masked) case is much simpler than it looked. **MDLM** (Sahoo et al.) and **MD4** (Shi et al.) derived that the continuous-time training bound is just a weighted average of ordinary masked-LM cross-entropy losses over different masking rates. **RADD** (Ou et al.) showed the model does not even need to know the noise level: the quantity it estimates equals the conditional probability of clean tokens times a known scalar, which links masked diffusion to *any-order* autoregressive models. With modern training recipes, MDLM approached AR perplexity at GPT-2 scale.

The practical upshot: a masked diffusion LM is a bidirectional transformer trained with a randomly varying mask ratio, sampled by iterative unmasking. That made it easy to scale with standard LLM infrastructure.

sections.heading: Scaling up: LLaDA, AR conversion and block diffusion
sections.md:
**LLaDA** (Nie et al., Renmin University and Ant Group, 2025) trained an 8B masked diffusion model from scratch with the standard pretrain then SFT pipeline. The authors report it is competitive with LLaMA3 8B on in-context learning and, notably, handles the *reversal curse* (it beat GPT-4o at completing reversed poem lines), a task where left-to-right training is structurally weak.

Training from scratch is expensive, so a parallel line converts AR checkpoints. Gong et al. (2024) turned GPT-2 and LLaMA models up to 7B into DiffuGPT and DiffuLLaMA with under 200B tokens of continued pretraining. **Dream 7B** (HKUNLP, 2025) used the same AR-initialization idea plus token-level noise rescheduling.

Two problems remained for speed. Bidirectional attention breaks the KV cache, because every position can change every step; and full-sequence diffusion needs a fixed output length. **Block diffusion** (Arriola et al., 2025) splits the output into blocks generated left to right, with diffusion inside each block, so finished blocks can be cached and lengths are flexible. **Fast-dLLM** (Wu et al., NVIDIA and HKU, 2025) added an approximate block-wise KV cache and a confidence threshold for parallel unmasking; the authors report up to 27.6x throughput on LLaDA and Dream. Their diagnosis of quality loss is worth remembering: decoding several tokens at once assumes they are independent given the context, which is false when they depend on each other.

sections.heading: Where it is now: block-wise, converted, and in products
sections.md:
Commercial use started with Inception Labs, whose technical report lists diffusion researchers Stefano Ermon, Aditya Grover and Volodymyr Kuleshov among its authors. The **Mercury** report (2025) describes Mercury Coder Mini and Small at 1109 and 737 tokens per second on H100s in independent measurements by Artificial Analysis. Google DeepMind showed **Gemini Diffusion** as an experimental demo in May 2025, listing 1479 tokens per second sampling speed and coding scores close to Gemini 2.0 Flash-Lite, with weaker science and reasoning scores. ByteDance's **Seed Diffusion Preview** (2025) reports 2,146 tokens per second on H20 GPUs for code.

The recent trend is convergence on block-wise generation from converted AR models. **LLaDA2.0** (Ant Group, December 2025) converts AR MoE models into 16B and 100B diffusion models with a warm-up, stable, decay schedule over block size. **Mercury 2** (Inception, February 2026) is a reasoning model; Inception reports 1,009 tokens per second on Blackwell GPUs and 128K context; **Mercury 3** (October 2026) scales the same approach to over 40 times Mercury 1's parameters, again with vendor-reported speeds above 1,000 tokens per second. NVIDIA's **Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion** (May 2026) trains one model jointly for AR and diffusion and uses diffusion to draft and AR to verify, a form of self-speculative decoding. **DiffusionGemma** (June 2026) is an open Apache 2.0 model built on Gemma 4 26B A4B that denoises 256-token canvases with up to 48 steps each.

The research side is questioning masking itself. Sahoo et al.'s 2026 scaling study finds that *uniform-state* diffusion (tokens are swapped for random tokens, so the model can revise any position) can be preferable despite worse perplexity, because it samples faster in few steps. Their follow-up, **Uno** (September 2026), keeps an AR model and adds small diffusion weights that draft tokens the AR distribution accepts losslessly; the authors report up to 3x speedups over the base model.

sections.heading: The honest tradeoffs
sections.md:
Speed claims depend heavily on setting. Diffusion wins most at low batch size, where AR decoding is memory bound and parallel token prediction uses idle compute. At high concurrency an AR server is already compute bound, so the advantage shrinks; that is why Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion keeps an AR mode and picks a mode by load.

Quality per token still usually trails the best AR models of the same size on reasoning-heavy benchmarks; Google's own Gemini Diffusion table shows it behind Flash-Lite on GPQA Diamond and BIG-Bench Extra Hard, and the DiffusionGemma card shows 69.1 versus 88.3 percent for its AR parent on AIME 2026. Most headline throughput numbers come from the model developers. And the field has quietly moved back toward AR structure (blocks, KV caches, AR initialization), so today's production diffusion LMs are best read as *semi-autoregressive*: sequential across blocks, parallel within them.

lineage.who: Shi, Han, Wang, Doucet, Titsias (Google DeepMind)
lineage.contribution: Independently derived the continuous-time masked diffusion bound as a weighted integral of cross-entropy losses, and added state-dependent masking schedules.

lineage.title: Your Absorbing Discrete Diffusion Secretly Models the Conditional Distributions of Clean Data (RADD)
lineage.who: Ou, Nie, Xue, Zhu, Sun, Li, Li (Renmin University)
lineage.contribution: Showed the absorbing-diffusion target is a time-independent conditional of clean data, so no time input is needed, and unified masked diffusion with any-order autoregressive models.

lineage.title: Scaling Diffusion Language Models via Adaptation from Autoregressive Models
lineage.who: Gong, Kong et al. (HKUNLP and collaborators)
lineage.contribution: Converted pretrained AR models (GPT-2, LLaMA up to 7B) into diffusion models DiffuGPT and DiffuLLaMA with under 200B tokens of continued pretraining.

lineage.title: Large Language Diffusion Models (LLaDA)
lineage.who: Nie et al., Renmin University and Ant Group
lineage.contribution: An 8B masked diffusion LM trained from scratch with pretraining and SFT; reported competitive with LLaMA3 8B on in-context learning and stronger on reversal tasks.

lineage.title: Block Diffusion: Interpolating Between Autoregressive and Diffusion Language Models
lineage.contribution: Generate blocks left to right with diffusion inside each block, enabling KV caching, flexible output length and parallel sampling within a block.

lineage.title: Fast-dLLM: Training-free Acceleration of Diffusion LLM
lineage.who: Wu et al., NVIDIA and HKU
lineage.contribution: Approximate block-wise KV cache for bidirectional models plus confidence-thresholded parallel decoding; reports up to 27.6x throughput on LLaDA and Dream.

lineage.title: Mercury: Ultra-Fast Language Models Based on Diffusion
lineage.contribution: Commercial-scale diffusion LLMs (Mercury Coder Mini and Small), measured at 1109 and 737 tokens per second on H100 by Artificial Analysis, with a public API.

lineage.title: Dream 7B: Diffusion Large Language Models
lineage.contribution: Open 7B diffusion LM initialized from an AR model, with context-adaptive token-level noise rescheduling; supports arbitrary-order generation and infilling.

frontier.title: Mercury 3
frontier.note: Inception's largest diffusion LLM, which it says has over 40x the parameters of Mercury 1, with 1M-token context. Inception reports 1,068 tokens per second on NVIDIA GPUs and quality on par with speed-optimized frontier models. Closed weights; all numbers are vendor-reported.

frontier.title: Uno: Unlocking Lossless Speedups in LLMs via Discrete Diffusion
frontier.who: Sahoo et al., MBZUAI IFM, Cornell Tech, Cerebras
frontier.note: Keeps a standard AR model and adds light diffusion weights, trained by distillation, that draft several tokens which the AR distribution then accepts losslessly. The authors report up to 3x speedups over the base AR model at every batch size tested, without the quality loss of pure diffusion LMs.

frontier.title: DiffusionGemma 26B A4B
frontier.note: Open-weight (Apache 2.0) diffusion model fine-tuned from Gemma 4 26B A4B MoE. It denoises 256-token canvases with up to 48 steps, then appends each canvas to the KV cache. The card reports 15 to 20 tokens per forward pass and over 1,100 tokens/s per user on an H100 (FP8), but it trails Gemma 4 on AIME 2026 (69.1 vs 88.3 percent).

frontier.title: Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion: a tri-mode language model
frontier.note: One model trained jointly for AR and diffusion decoding, plus self-speculation where the diffusion mode drafts and the AR mode verifies. NVIDIA reports the 8B model decodes 5.9x more tokens per forward than Qwen3-8B and 4x throughput on GB200.

frontier.title: Mercury 2
frontier.note: A commercial diffusion reasoning model with tunable reasoning and 128K context. Inception reports 1,009 tokens per second on NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs. Weights are closed; the numbers are vendor-reported.

frontier.title: Scaling Beyond Masked Diffusion Language Models
frontier.note: First scaling-law study of uniform-state and interpolating discrete diffusion. Finds perplexity misleads across diffusion families: at 1.7B, uniform-state diffusion beats AR and masked diffusion on GSM8K despite worse perplexity, because it samples well in few steps.

frontier.title: LLaDA2.0: Scaling Up Diffusion Language Models to 100B
frontier.who: Bie et al., Ant Group and collaborators
frontier.note: Converts pretrained AR MoE models into open 16B and 100B diffusion models with a warm-up, stable, decay schedule over block size (small blocks, full sequence, then small blocks again), then SFT and DPO.

frontier.title: Seed Diffusion Preview
frontier.note: Large discrete-state diffusion model for code; reports 2,146 tokens per second on H20 GPUs with competitive code benchmark scores.

open: Can diffusion LMs match AR models on long multi-step reasoning at equal compute, or is left-to-right order a useful inductive bias for reasoning?
How should many tokens be committed at once without violating dependencies between them? Confidence thresholds are heuristics.
Does the speed advantage survive at high serving concurrency, where AR decoding is already compute bound?
Masked or uniform-state? Masked diffusion cannot revise a committed token; uniform-state can self-correct but has worse likelihood.
What is the right RL recipe for diffusion LMs, given that sequence log-likelihoods are only available as bounds?

connects.why: Both attack the one-token-per-pass bottleneck; Nemotron-Labs-Diffusion uses a diffusion mode as the drafter for its own AR verifier.
Text diffusion borrows its core ideas (forward noising, learned reverse process, consistency distillation) from image diffusion.
Block diffusion exists largely to restore KV caching; the throughput story depends on batch size and serving setup.
Applying GRPO-style RL to diffusion LMs (d1, diffu-GRPO) needs new likelihood estimates, an active area.

threads.title: Tokenization and the move to byte-level models
threads.dek: Almost every LLM still reads text through a fixed vocabulary learned by a 1990s compression trick. Byte-level models with learned patches are finally matching it, and the tokenizer may end up inside the network.

sections.heading: Why a frozen vocabulary sits in front of every model
sections.md:
A language model does not see characters. A **tokenizer** first splits text into pieces from a fixed vocabulary (for GPT-2, 50,257 entries) and the model only ever sees the integer IDs. Tokenization exists because raw bytes make sequences several times longer, and attention cost grows with sequence length; grouping frequent byte runs into one token is cheap compression.

The costs are real and well documented. The same sentence translated into different languages can take very different numbers of tokens: Petrov et al. (2023) measured differences of up to 15x, which means some languages pay more per API call, get less context and wait longer. Tokens that exist in the vocabulary but barely appear in training data, the "glitch tokens" made famous by `SolidGoldMagikarp`, can trigger bizarre behaviour; Land and Bartolo (2024) built automatic detectors and found such tokens across many models. And because the model never sees letters, character-level tasks such as spelling and counting become oddly hard.

The tokenizer is also trained separately, before the model, and then frozen. Whatever segmentation choices it made are permanent.

sections.heading: BPE, WordPiece and the byte-level compromise
sections.md:
**Byte pair encoding** (BPE) began as a data compression algorithm. Sennrich, Haddow and Birch (2015) repurposed it for neural machine translation: start from characters, repeatedly merge the most frequent adjacent pair into a new symbol, and stop at a target vocabulary size. Rare words become sequences of subword units, so the model has an open vocabulary. They report gains of 1.1 and 1.3 BLEU over a dictionary back-off on English-German and English-Russian.

Google's neural translation system (Wu et al., 2016) used a similar *wordpiece* model. Kudo (2018) proposed a **unigram language model** tokenizer that keeps a probabilistic vocabulary and can sample different segmentations of the same text as regularization. **SentencePiece** (Kudo and Richardson, 2018) packaged BPE and unigram into a language-independent library that treats whitespace as an ordinary symbol, which is why it became standard for multilingual models.

GPT-2 (Radford et al., 2019) made the choice most modern LLMs inherit: **byte-level BPE**. Unicode has over 130,000 code points, so a character-level base vocabulary is huge; running BPE over UTF-8 bytes needs only 256 base symbols and can encode any string. The GPT-2 paper also notes a failure mode of greedy merging (spending vocabulary on `dog.`, `dog!` and `dog?`) and fixes it by forbidding merges across character categories, with an exception for spaces. That pre-tokenization rule, splitting on spaces and punctuation before merging, is still in most tokenizers.

sections.heading: Dropping the tokenizer: bytes, then patches
sections.md:
Token-free models came first from encoders. **CANINE** (Clark et al., Google, 2021) read characters and downsampled them inside the network. **ByT5** (Xue et al., 2021) showed a nearly unmodified T5 can run on raw bytes, competitive with token models and much more robust to typos and noise, but paying in sequence length and FLOPs.

For decoders the length problem is worse, so the next step was hierarchy. **MegaByte** (Yu et al., Meta, 2023) cut the byte stream into fixed-size patches: a large global model runs once per patch and a small local model predicts the bytes inside it. **MambaByte** (Wang et al., 2024) instead used a Mamba state space model, whose memory does not grow with sequence length. **SpaceByte** (Slagle, 2024) noticed that fixed patches ignore word structure and inserted the large blocks only after space-like bytes, roughly matching tokenized models at equal compute.

The **Byte Latent Transformer** (BLT, Pagnoni et al., Meta, 2024) made patching *dynamic*. A small byte model estimates the entropy of the next byte; a new patch starts where the next byte is hard to predict, so predictable stretches become long cheap patches and surprising ones get more compute. BLT reported the first FLOP-controlled scaling study of byte models up to 8B parameters and 4T training bytes, matching Llama 3 training-FLOP-controlled performance while offering up to 50 percent fewer inference FLOPs. The BLT paper reports that SpaceByte-style space patching improved on MegaByte but stayed well behind Llama 3; architectural changes (hash n-gram embeddings, cross-attention) and dynamic patching together closed the gap.

sections.heading: Predicting further ahead: multi-token prediction
sections.md:
A related question is the unit of *prediction*, not just of input. Gloeckle et al. (Meta, 2024) trained models to predict the next n tokens with n output heads on a shared trunk. The authors report that their 13B model solves 12 percent more HumanEval and 17 percent more MBPP problems than a next-token baseline, and that 4-token models decode up to 3x faster by using the extra heads for self-speculation.

DeepSeek-V3 (December 2024) adopted a multi-token prediction (MTP) objective, citing Gloeckle et al. as inspiration but predicting the extra tokens sequentially so each depth keeps the full causal chain. It is used to densify the training signal and can be reused as a draft for speculative decoding.

Both ideas push against the same constraint: one fixed-size token per step is an arbitrary granularity. Hierarchical byte models let the model choose bigger units where text is easy; MTP lets it commit to more than one unit per step.

sections.heading: Where it is now: learned chunking and retrofitting
sections.md:
Three directions dominate the last 18 months.

**Better tokens, same pipeline.** SuperBPE (Liu et al., 2025) lets BPE learn "superwords" that cross whitespace after a first subword stage. At a fixed 200k vocabulary it encodes text with up to 33 percent fewer tokens; an 8B model trained with it improved by 4.0 points on average over 30 tasks and needed 27 percent less inference compute, per the authors.

**Learned segmentation inside the model.** Meta's AU-Net (Videau et al., 2025) pools bytes into words, word pairs and longer spans in an autoregressive U-Net. H-Net (Hwang, Wang and Gu, 2025) learns content-dependent chunk boundaries end to end; the authors report a one-stage byte H-Net beats a BPE Transformer at matched compute, and a two-stage one matches a Transformer twice its size, with larger gains on Chinese, code and DNA. Scratchpad Patching (Zheng et al., 2026) targets the main cost of large patches, "patch lag", and reports near byte-level quality at 16 bytes per patch with a 16x smaller patch KV cache.

**Retrofitting instead of retraining.** Ai2's Bolmo (December 2025) converts Olmo 3 7B into a byte-level model: train new byte encoder, boundary predictor and decoder around the frozen transformer, then fine-tune everything, about 49B tokens in total. Ai2 reports it stays close to Olmo 3 overall and gains nearly 20 points on character-level tasks. Aleph Alpha (March 2026) did the same at larger scale, converting Llama 3.1 8B and 70B into hierarchical byte-level models that pool bytes into word embeddings. A late 2026 study (Wang et al.) even argues plain byte Transformers, with the right training tricks, scale better than subword ones and learn their own segmentation positions.

sections.heading: What production still does
sections.md:
Despite the progress, widely deployed LLMs still use subword vocabularies, typically byte-level BPE in the GPT-2 tradition, because the whole stack (pretraining data pipelines, KV cache sizing, pricing per token, speculative decoding) assumes them. Byte models change throughput characteristics: Ai2 reports Bolmo at roughly 125 bytes per second versus 150 for the subword model at the same compression.

The likely path is incremental. Retrofitting existing checkpoints avoids paying for a new pretraining run, and learned chunking can be introduced as a layer rather than a rewrite. Tokenizer-free results are still mostly at the 1B to 8B scale; the largest byte-level models so far are Aleph Alpha's 2026 conversions of Llama 3.1 8B and 70B. No frontier-scale model has been pretrained on bytes from scratch, so claims that bytes beat tokens at that scale remain unproven.

open: Do byte-level and learned-chunking models keep their advantage at frontier scale (hundreds of billions of parameters), or only up to the 8B to 70B range tested so far?
Can a single learned segmentation serve all languages and modalities fairly, removing the up to 15x cost gap between languages?
How should serving, pricing and KV cache budgets work when the unit of computation is a variable-size patch rather than a token?
Is retrofitting (Bolmo-style) enough, or do the benefits of bytes only appear when pretraining from scratch?
How far ahead should a model predict? Multi-token prediction and hierarchical byte models both suggest next-token is not the right granularity.

connects.why: Tokenization is largely a workaround for the cost of attention over long sequences; cheaper attention changes the byte-level tradeoff.
MambaByte and H-Net use state space layers to make long byte sequences affordable.
Multi-token prediction heads double as drafters, and byte models use tokenized drafts for speculative decoding.
Tokenizers are trained on a data mix and inherit its language balance; glitch tokens come from mismatches between tokenizer and training data.

threads.title: Learned memory and adaptive depth: test-time training and looped models
threads.dek: Two ideas loosen the fixed shape of a Transformer: layers whose memory is a small model trained while it reads, and blocks reused in a loop so a model can think for more steps without more parameters.

sections.heading: Two fixed budgets a Transformer cannot change
sections.md:
A standard Transformer has two budgets set at design time. The first is **memory**: attention keeps every past key and value, so recall is exact but each new token costs time proportional to the context. Recurrent layers keep a fixed-size state instead, which is cheap but fills up. The TTT paper (Sun et al., 2024) shows what that limit looks like: on long documents, a Transformer's perplexity keeps falling as context grows to 32k tokens, while Mamba's stops improving after about 16k.

The second budget is **depth**. A token passes through each of $L$ layers exactly once, so the model gets a fixed number of sequential steps of computation before it must predict. Problems that need many steps, such as following a chain of references or adding many numbers, either need more layers (more parameters) or explicit chain-of-thought tokens.

This thread follows two lines of work that attack these budgets with the same tool, **reuse with learning**:

- **Learned memory.** Make the recurrent state the weights of a small model, and update it by gradient descent on the context as it streams in. This is test-time training (TTT), and Titans is its best-known descendant.
- **Adaptive depth.** Apply one block of layers many times, so depth becomes a knob you set at inference. This runs from Universal Transformers to today's looped language models.

Both trade wall-clock time and training complexity for flexibility, and both are still mostly tested at small scale.

sections.heading: Memory as a model you train while reading
sections.md:
The roots are **fast weights**. Schlag, Irie and Schmidhuber (2021) showed linear attention is a fast weight memory: a matrix rewritten at every token by adding outer products of values and keys. They also proposed a delta-rule write that corrects what is stored instead of only adding.

**TTT layers** (Sun et al., 2024) generalized that view. The hidden state is the weights $W$ of a small model $f$, linear in TTT-Linear or a two-layer MLP in TTT-MLP. Each token takes one gradient step on a self-supervised loss, $\lVert f(\theta_K x_t; W) - \theta_V x_t\rVert^2$, and the output is $f(\theta_Q x_t; W)$. The projections play the roles of key, value and query, and they are learned in an outer loop by ordinary next-token training, a form of meta-learning. With a linear model and batch size 1, one gradient step is exactly the delta rule. For speed the paper takes gradients in mini-batches of 16 tokens and computes each block with matmuls.

**Titans** (Behrouz, Zhong and Mirrokni, Google Research, December 2024) asked what a good long-term memory needs. Its memory is a deeper MLP trained the same way, but the update uses momentum, so a surprising event keeps being written for several tokens after it, and a forget gate that decays old content. Titans pairs this memory with attention, which acts as precise short-term memory, and with learned persistent tokens. The authors report better results than Transformer++ and recent linear recurrent baselines at 340M to 760M parameters, and needle-in-a-haystack retrieval beyond 2M tokens.

The same group's **Miras** framework (April 2025) then described linear attention, DeltaNet, Gated DeltaNet, TTT and Titans as choices along four axes: memory architecture, inner objective ("attentional bias"), retention or forgetting, and the inner optimizer.

sections.heading: Depth as a loop: from Universal Transformers to latent reasoning
sections.md:
**Adaptive Computation Time** (Graves, DeepMind, 2016) let an RNN learn how many internal steps to take per input, using a halting probability and a small "ponder" cost. **Universal Transformers** (Dehghani, Gouws, Vinyals, Uszkoreit and Kaiser, 2018) brought this to Transformers: one block with shared weights is applied repeatedly to all positions, each position can halt on its own with ACT, and a timestep embedding tells the block which step it is on. The authors showed UTs generalize better on algorithmic tasks and are Turing-complete under certain assumptions. **ALBERT** (Lan et al., Google, 2019) used cross-layer parameter sharing mainly to shrink BERT, citing UT as a related strategy.

Interest returned with reasoning models. **Relaxed Recursive Transformers** (Bae et al., Google DeepMind and KAIST, 2024) converted pretrained LLMs into looped models with a shared block plus small per-loop LoRA adapters. **Huginn** (Geiping et al., 2025) pretrained a 3.5B-parameter recurrent-depth model on 800B tokens: a prelude embeds the input, a 4-layer core block is looped a random number of times during training, and a coda decodes. Re-injecting the input at every loop and not telling the block its step number made it extrapolate to more loops. The authors report reasoning gains up to compute equivalent to 50B parameters, and per-token early exit without special training.

**Saunshi et al.** (Google Research, 2025) gave the theory and controlled evidence: on many reasoning tasks a $k$-layer block looped $L$ times nearly matches a $kL$-layer model, while gains on memorization-heavy tasks are much smaller. The pattern repeats across papers: looping adds depth for reasoning, not capacity for facts.

sections.heading: Where it is now: scaling, honest accounting, and end-to-end TTT
sections.md:
**Learned memory.** *Test-Time Training Done Right* (LaCT, Zhang et al., May 2025) found earlier TTT layers often used under 5% of GPU peak FLOPs, so it updates fast weights once per huge chunk (2K to 1M tokens) with window attention inside the chunk. The paper reports up to 70% GPU utilization and nonlinear fast weights as large as 40% of model parameters. Google's **Nested Learning** work (NeurIPS 2025, blog November 2025) treats a model as nested optimization problems updated at different frequencies; its proof-of-concept **Hope** extends Titans with multi-frequency memory blocks and self-modification. **TTT-E2E** (Tandon, Dalal et al., December 2025) goes furthest: a standard Transformer with sliding-window attention keeps training on the context by next-token prediction at test time, with an initialization meta-learned for that. For 3B models on 164B tokens, the authors report it scales with context like full attention, unlike Mamba 2 and Gated DeltaNet, while running 2.7x faster than full attention at 128K tokens.

**Adaptive depth.** **Mixture-of-Recursions** (Bae et al., July 2025) adds routers that give each token its own number of loops and caches KV only for active tokens. **Ouro** (Zhu et al., October 2025) pretrained looped models on 7.7T tokens with an entropy-regularized learned depth; the authors report 1.4B and 2.6B models matching up to 12B models on many benchmarks, with the advantage coming from knowledge manipulation rather than capacity. Then came the accounting. An iso-depth scaling-law study (Schwethelm, Rueckert and Kaissis, April 2026) estimates one loop of a block is worth $r^{0.46}$ unique blocks: at $r = 4$ a 410M looped model matched a 580M plain one but cost as much to train as a 1B model. In July 2026 the **Loopie** authors claimed the opposite outcome for their looped MoE models, reporting they beat compute-matched vanilla baselines. Whether loops pay for their training compute is now the central empirical question.
