lineage.contribution: Recast linear attention as a fast weight memory rewritten every token, and introduced a delta-rule write that corrects stored associations. The direct ancestor of treating a layer's state as trainable weights.

lineage.title: Learning to (Learn at Test Time): RNNs with Expressive Hidden States
lineage.contribution: Made the hidden state a linear model or MLP updated by a gradient step on a learned self-supervised loss, with mini-batch and dual forms for speed. Unlike Mamba, kept improving with context past 16k tokens.

lineage.title: Relaxed Recursive Transformers: Effective Parameter Sharing with Layer-wise LoRA
lineage.who: Bae, Fisch, Harutyunyan, Ji, Kim, Schuster (Google DeepMind, KAIST)
lineage.contribution: Converted pretrained LLMs into looped models that repeat one block, relaxed by per-loop LoRA adapters; recursive Gemma 1B recovered most of Gemma 2B's quality. Proposed continuous depth-wise batching.

lineage.title: Titans: Learning to Memorize at Test Time
lineage.contribution: A deep neural long-term memory trained at test time with momentum (carrying surprise forward) and a forget gate, combined with attention as short-term memory. Reported gains at small scale and retrieval beyond 2M tokens.

lineage.title: Scaling up Test-Time Compute with Latent Reasoning: A Recurrent Depth Approach (Huginn)
lineage.who: Geiping, McLeish, Jain et al. (ELLIS Tuebingen, U. Maryland, LLNL)
lineage.contribution: Pretrained a 3.5B prelude, looped core and coda model on 800B tokens with random loop counts and truncated backprop, so test-time loops scale reasoning up to compute equivalent to 50B parameters.

lineage.title: Reasoning with Latent Thoughts: On the Power of Looped Transformers
lineage.who: Saunshi, Dikkala, Li, Kumar, Reddi (Google Research)
lineage.contribution: Showed theoretically and empirically that many reasoning problems need depth, not parameters: a k-layer block looped L times nearly matches a kL-layer model, and looped models can simulate chain-of-thought steps.

lineage.title: It's All Connected: Test-Time Memorization, Attentional Bias, Retention, and Online Optimization (Miras)
lineage.contribution: Unified Transformers, Titans and linear RNNs as associative memories defined by four choices (memory architecture, attentional bias objective, retention gate, learning algorithm) and proposed new variants.

lineage.title: Test-Time Training Done Right (LaCT)
lineage.who: Zhang, Bi, Hong et al. (MIT, Adobe Research)
lineage.contribution: Updated fast weights once per very large chunk with window attention inside, raising GPU utilization from often under 5% to up to 70% and allowing fast-weight memories up to 40% of model size.

lineage.title: Mixture-of-Recursions: Learning Dynamic Recursive Depths for Adaptive Token-Level Computation
lineage.who: Bae, Kim, Bayat et al. (KAIST, Google DeepMind, Mila)
lineage.contribution: Added lightweight routers that give each token its own recursion depth in a shared-block model, caching KV only for active tokens. Reported a better perplexity and throughput frontier from 135M to 1.7B parameters.

lineage.title: Scaling Latent Reasoning via Looped Language Models (Ouro)
lineage.who: Zhu, Wang, Hua et al. (ByteDance Seed and others)
lineage.contribution: Pretrained looped language models on 7.7T tokens with an entropy-regularized objective for learned depth. The authors report 1.4B and 2.6B models matching up to 12B models, driven by knowledge manipulation, not capacity.

lineage.title: End-to-End Test-Time Training for Long Context (TTT-E2E)
lineage.who: Tandon, Dalal, Li et al. (with Yu Sun)
lineage.contribution: Treated long context as continual learning: a sliding-window Transformer keeps training on the context by next-token prediction at test time, with a meta-learned initialization, instead of using a special memory layer.

frontier.title: Loop the Loopies! Looped MoE models
frontier.who: Gao, Chen, Xiao et al. (IQuest Research)
frontier.note: Two looped MoE models (20B total with 2B active, 6B with 0.6B active). The authors claim, against the usual finding, that they substantially beat vanilla baselines trained with the same compute, including a 30B-A3B model. Independent checks are pending.

frontier.title: How Much Is One Recurrence Worth? Iso-depth scaling laws
frontier.note: Fits a scaling law in which r loops of a block count as r^0.46 unique blocks: at r = 4 a 410M looped model matches a 580M plain model but costs as much to train as a 1B one. Truncated backprop lowers the exponent to 0.38; hyperconnections raise it to 0.65.

frontier.title: End-to-End Test-Time Training for Long Context
frontier.who: Tandon, Dalal et al. (with Yu Sun)
frontier.note: A sliding-window Transformer that learns from its context at test time. For 3B models on 164B tokens the authors report it scales with context like full attention, unlike Mamba 2 and Gated DeltaNet, and runs 2.7x faster than full attention at 128K.

frontier.title: Nested Learning and the Hope architecture
frontier.note: Frames a model as nested optimization problems updated at different frequencies. Hope, a self-modifying variant of Titans with a continuum of memory modules, is reported to beat Titans, Samba and a Transformer on language modeling and common-sense reasoning, and to outperform TTT and Mamba2 (roughly matching Titans) on needle-in-a-haystack retrieval.

frontier.title: Scaling Latent Reasoning via Looped Language Models (Ouro)
frontier.who: Zhu, Wang, Hua et al. (ByteDance Seed and others)
frontier.note: Pretrains looped models on 7.7T tokens with learned depth allocation. The authors report small models matching much larger ones and argue the gain is better use of knowledge, not more stored knowledge.

frontier.title: Mixture-of-Recursions
frontier.who: Bae, Kim, Bayat et al. (KAIST, Google DeepMind, Mila)
frontier.note: Combines parameter sharing with per-token depth chosen by routers, and only tokens still active at a depth attend and cache keys and values there, attacking the latency and cache costs of looping.

frontier.title: Test-Time Training Done Right (LaCT)
frontier.who: Zhang, Bi, Hong et al. (MIT, Adobe Research)
frontier.note: Large-chunk updates make TTT hardware-efficient (up to 70% GPU utilization reported) and let fast weights grow to 40% of model size, with uses in long video generation and novel view synthesis.

open: Do looped models pay for their training compute? An iso-depth scaling study says one loop is worth about r^0.46 unique blocks, while Loopie claims compute-matched wins. Which conditions decide it?
Test-time-trained memories are mostly evaluated below a few billion parameters. Do their long-context advantages hold at frontier scale and on agentic workloads?
Learning at test time costs wall-clock time and memory traffic. Can kernels make deep memories and many loops as fast as attention or Gated DeltaNet in practice?
How should a model decide how many loops or how much memory update a token deserves, and how do variable depths work with batched serving?
If a model updates its weights while reading, what are the safety and reproducibility implications of behavior that depends on everything it has seen?

connects.why: DeltaNet and Gated DeltaNet are the simplest test-time-trained memories: one gradient step on a linear model per token, with decay as weight decay.
Titans, LaCT and TTT-E2E keep attention as precise short-term memory and rely on fast attention kernels inside chunks or windows.
Looping and MoE both decouple parameters from per-token compute, and recent looped models such as Loopie are themselves MoE.

threads.title: Optimizers and scaling recipes: Adam to Muon, muP and WSD schedules
threads.dek: For a decade nearly every large model trained with AdamW. Now matrix-aware optimizers like Muon train trillion-parameter models, and recipes like muP, WSD schedules and scaling laws decide if the gains survive scale.

sections.heading: Why the optimizer recipe is worth millions
sections.md:
A pretraining run is a single shot: you choose model size, token count, learning rate, schedule and optimizer before spending most of the budget, and you cannot afford to tune them at full scale. Two kinds of research address this. **Scaling laws** predict how loss depends on parameters, data and compute so you can pick the size and token count. **Optimizers and parametrizations** decide how much loss each step buys and whether hyperparameters found on a small model still work on a large one.

The stakes are large but easy to overstate. Moonshot AI reports that Muon reaches about 2x the compute efficiency of AdamW in its compute-optimal scaling experiments. A careful controlled study (Wen et al., 2025) found that once every baseline is properly tuned, the speedup of the best alternatives over AdamW shrinks from 1.4x at 0.1B parameters to 1.1x at 1.2B. Both can be true in their own settings, and the gap between them is the story of this thread.

sections.heading: Adam, AdamW and the scaling-law era
sections.md:
**Adam** (Kingma and Ba, 2014) keeps running averages of each parameter's gradient and squared gradient, and divides the first by the square root of the second. Every coordinate gets its own step size, which makes Adam robust to badly scaled problems. Loshchilov and Hutter (2017) noticed that implementing weight decay as an L2 penalty interacts badly with that per-coordinate scaling, and proposed **AdamW**, which applies decay directly to the weights. AdamW became the default for transformers.

**Scaling laws** then set the budget. Kaplan et al. (OpenAI, 2020) found loss falls as a power law in model size, data and compute across more than seven orders of magnitude, and concluded the compute-optimal move was very large models trained on relatively little data. Hoffmann et al. (DeepMind, 2022) redid the analysis with over 400 models and found parameters and tokens should grow *equally*: their 70B **Chinchilla**, trained on 4x more data than the 280B Gopher with the same compute, beat it across the board. Hoffmann et al. attribute part of the disagreement to Kaplan's use of one fixed learning rate schedule for all runs; they found the best final loss comes from matching the cosine schedule to each run's token count.

That detail hints at the hidden cost of cosine decay: the schedule depends on the final step count, so every point on a scaling curve needs its own run.

sections.heading: Transferring hyperparameters and decoupling the schedule
sections.md:
Greg Yang and Edward Hu (2020) showed that under the standard parametrization, very wide networks stop learning features, and proposed a fix they named the **maximal update parametrization** (muP): scale initializations and per-layer learning rates with width so each layer's update has the right size regardless of width. **Tensor Programs V** (Yang et al., Microsoft and OpenAI, 2022) turned this into *muTransfer*: tune on a small proxy, copy the hyperparameters to the large model. The paper reports beating published GPT-3 6.7B numbers using hyperparameters from a 40M model, at a tuning cost of 7 percent of pretraining. Yang, Simon and Bernstein (2023) later restated muP as a rule about the spectral norm of weight updates, which matters for Muon below.

**Warmup-stable-decay** (WSD) removes the schedule's dependence on run length. MiniCPM (Hu et al., 2024) held the learning rate constant for most of training and decayed it only in a short final phase, so one long run can be branched into many decayed checkpoints. Hagele et al. (2024) showed constant LR plus cooldown scales as reliably as cosine and lets scaling-law experiments reuse runs. MiniCPM used it to fit data-model scaling laws cheaply and reported a compute-optimal tokens-per-parameter ratio well above Chinchilla's. Not everyone switched: the GLM-4.5 report says WSD-trained models did worse on general benchmarks (SimpleQA, MMLU) in its early experiments, which the team read as underfitting, so it kept cosine decay.

sections.heading: From diagonal to matrix preconditioning: Shampoo, SOAP, Muon
sections.md:
Adam treats a weight matrix as a bag of independent numbers. **Shampoo** (Gupta, Koren and Singer, Google, 2018) keeps one preconditioner per tensor dimension, a left and a right matrix for each weight matrix, approximating full-matrix AdaGrad at manageable cost. It was hard to engineer; Meta's distributed PyTorch Shampoo (Shi et al., 2023) brought per-step overhead within 10 percent of Adam, and a Distributed Shampoo submission won the external-tuning track of the first AlgoPerf training-algorithms competition.

**SOAP** (Vyas et al., 2024) showed Shampoo is equivalent to running Adafactor in Shampoo's eigenbasis, and proposed running Adam in that slowly rotating basis instead. The authors report over 40 percent fewer iterations than AdamW at large batch sizes.

**Muon** (Keller Jordan and collaborators, December 2024) is simpler. Take the SGD-momentum update for each hidden-layer matrix and approximately replace it with the nearest orthogonal matrix ($UV^\top$ from its SVD), computed with five Newton-Schulz iterations in bfloat16. Embeddings, output head and vectors stay on AdamW. The motivation came from Bernstein and Newhouse (2024), who showed Shampoo without accumulation is steepest descent under the spectral norm. Muon set records in the NanoGPT and CIFAR-10 speedruns.

Moonshot AI's **Moonlight** (2025) found two fixes needed at scale, weight decay and matching the update RMS to AdamW's, and trained a 16B MoE on 5.7T tokens. **Kimi K2** (2025) then hit exploding attention logits with Muon and added **QK-Clip**, which rescales query and key weights whenever a head's max logit gets too large; the 1T-parameter model trained on 15.5T tokens with zero loss spikes.

sections.heading: Where it is now: Muon at frontier scale, and honest benchmarks
sections.md:
Matrix optimizers moved from speedruns to flagship models within about a year. **GLM-4.5** (Zhipu AI, August 2025) used Muon for all parameters except embeddings, biases and RMSNorm weights in a 355B MoE. **DeepSeek-V4** (April 2026) uses Muon for most modules, keeping AdamW for the embedding, prediction head and norms, and replaces the standard five Newton-Schulz steps with ten in two stages: eight fast-converging steps, then two that pin singular values at 1. It skips QK-Clip because it normalizes queries and keys directly.

Recipes for combining these optimizers with muP are maturing. Essential AI (2025) found Muon keeps data efficiency at batch sizes far beyond AdamW's critical batch size and paired it with muP for transfer. NVIDIA's **SOAP, Muon, and Beyond** (July 2026) reports both beat AdamW on multi-billion-parameter models trained on trillions of tokens, staying stable at batches up to 100M tokens where AdamW degrades.

Two cautions temper the excitement. Wen et al. (2025) found claimed speedups shrink with scale when baselines are tuned fairly and comparisons are made at the end of training. Qiu et al. (December 2025) argue the shrinkage partly reflects badly transferred hyperparameters: with muP-style learning rates and weight decay scaled as 1/width, they report Muon, SOAP and Shampoo hold a near 1.4x speedup over AdamW from 190M to 1.4B parameters. And **Spectral Scaling Laws of Muon** (MIT, June 2026) measured how momentum singular values shrink with model size and predicts some late layers will fall outside what five Newton-Schulz steps can orthogonalize at frontier scale. The authors note that DeepSeek-V4 already uses a 10-step composition, though DeepSeek's own stated reason is to pin singular values precisely at 1.

lineage.title: Adam: A Method for Stochastic Optimization
lineage.contribution: Per-coordinate adaptive step sizes from running averages of the gradient and squared gradient; became the default optimizer for deep learning.

lineage.title: Decoupled Weight Decay Regularization (AdamW)
lineage.contribution: Showed L2 regularization is not weight decay under Adam, and decoupled the decay from the gradient step. The standard transformer optimizer since.

lineage.title: Shampoo: Preconditioned Stochastic Tensor Optimization
lineage.who: Vineet Gupta, Tomer Koren, Yoram Singer (Google)
lineage.contribution: One preconditioner per tensor dimension, a Kronecker-factored approximation of full-matrix AdaGrad, at per-step cost comparable to Adam.

lineage.title: Scaling Laws for Neural Language Models
lineage.contribution: Loss follows power laws in parameters, data and compute over seven orders of magnitude; argued for very large models trained on modest data.

lineage.title: Feature Learning in Infinite-Width Neural Networks (Tensor Programs IV)
lineage.contribution: Showed standard and NTK parametrizations lose feature learning at large width and proposed the maximal update parametrization (muP) to restore it.

lineage.title: Training Compute-Optimal Large Language Models (Chinchilla)
lineage.contribution: From 400+ runs: scale parameters and tokens equally. The 70B Chinchilla with 4x more data beat the 280B Gopher at the same compute.

lineage.title: Tensor Programs V: Tuning Large Neural Networks via Zero-Shot Hyperparameter Transfer
lineage.contribution: muTransfer: tune hyperparameters on a small muP model and reuse them at scale; beat published GPT-3 6.7B numbers with tuning at 7 percent of pretraining cost.

lineage.title: A Distributed Data-Parallel PyTorch Implementation of Distributed Shampoo
lineage.contribution: Made Shampoo practical at scale with DTensor sharding, within 10 percent of Adam's per-step wall-clock; basis of the AlgoPerf-winning submission.

lineage.title: MiniCPM: Scalable Training Strategies (warmup-stable-decay)
lineage.contribution: Introduced the WSD learning rate schedule for continuous training and cheap data-model scaling studies, and used Tensor Program hyperparameter transfer.

lineage.title: Scaling Laws and Compute-Optimal Training Beyond Fixed Training Durations
lineage.who: Hagele, Bakouch, Kosson, Ben Allal, Von Werra, Jaggi
lineage.contribution: Showed constant learning rate plus cooldown (WSD) scales as reliably as cosine, so scaling-law sweeps can reuse runs instead of training one per budget.

lineage.title: SOAP: Improving and Stabilizing Shampoo using Adam
lineage.who: Vyas, Morwani, Zhao, Kwun, Shapira, Brandfonbrener, Janson, Kakade
lineage.contribution: Shampoo equals Adafactor in Shampoo's eigenbasis; SOAP runs Adam there instead. Reports over 40 percent fewer iterations than AdamW at large batch.

lineage.title: Old Optimizer, New Norm: An Anthology
lineage.contribution: Recast Adam and Shampoo (without averaging) as steepest descent under particular norms, arguing each layer type should get its own operator norm.

lineage.title: Muon: An optimizer for hidden layers in neural networks
lineage.contribution: Orthogonalize each hidden-layer momentum update with five Newton-Schulz iterations; set NanoGPT and CIFAR-10 speedrun records.

lineage.title: Muon is Scalable for LLM Training (Moonlight)
lineage.contribution: Added weight decay and AdamW-matched update RMS so Muon works at scale; reports about 2x compute efficiency over AdamW and trains a 16B MoE on 5.7T tokens.

lineage.title: Kimi K2: Open Agentic Intelligence (MuonClip)
lineage.contribution: QK-Clip rescales query and key weights when attention logits grow too large; trained a 1T-parameter MoE on 15.5T tokens with zero loss spikes.

frontier.title: SOAP, Muon, and Beyond: Pushing LLM Pretraining Scales
frontier.note: Fixes SOAP instabilities at large batch with per-step QR, compares optimizers with update-RMS matching, and reports SOAP and Muon beat AdamW on multi-billion-parameter, trillion-token runs, stable at batches up to 100M tokens. Ships a Megatron-compatible layer-wise distributed optimizer.

frontier.title: Spectral Scaling Laws of Muon
frontier.note: Tracks singular values of Muon's momentum from 77M to 2.8B parameters. Most layers scale mildly, but some late layers shrink fast enough that the standard 5-step Newton-Schulz would fail at frontier scale without more steps or retuned coefficients.

frontier.title: DeepSeek-V4: Towards Highly Efficient Million-Token Context Intelligence
frontier.note: Moves a frontier MoE family to Muon for most modules, with hybrid 10-step Newton-Schulz (8 fast steps, then 2 stabilizing steps) and query-key normalization instead of QK-Clip. AdamW stays on embeddings, head and norms.

frontier.title: Hyperparameter Transfer Enables Consistent Gains of Matrix-Preconditioned Optimizers Across Scales
frontier.note: Studies how learning rate and weight decay should scale with width and depth for Shampoo, SOAP and Muon. With muP-style learning rates, blocking or spectral normalization, and weight decay scaled as 1/width, the authors report a near 1.4x speedup over AdamW from 190M to 1.4B parameters that vanishes under incorrect scaling.

frontier.title: Fantastic Pretraining Optimizers and Where to Find Them
frontier.note: Ten optimizers, four scales, 1 to 8x Chinchilla data, all carefully tuned. Matrix preconditioners (Muon, SOAP) are fastest, but speedup over tuned AdamW falls from 1.4x at 0.1B to 1.1x at 1.2B, and rankings can flip before decay ends.

frontier.title: GLM-4.5 technical report
frontier.note: Trains a 355B-parameter MoE with Muon on all parameters except embeddings, biases and RMSNorm weights, and reports choosing cosine over WSD because WSD underfit on general benchmarks.

frontier.title: Practical Efficiency of Muon for Pretraining
frontier.note: Muon keeps data efficiency at batch sizes far beyond AdamW's critical batch size, expanding the compute-time Pareto frontier; pairs Muon with muP via a telescoping tuning procedure up to 4B parameters.

frontier.title: Accelerating Neural Network Training: An Analysis of the AlgoPerf Competition
frontier.note: Distributed Shampoo won the external-tuning track on wall-clock time-to-result across workloads, evidence that non-diagonal preconditioning pays off even with its overhead. Schedule-free AdamW won the self-tuning track.

open: Does the advantage of Muon and SOAP over tuned AdamW grow, shrink or vanish at frontier scale? Lab reports and controlled studies disagree.
What is the right parametrization for Muon (muP, spectral rules, update-RMS matching), and can hyperparameters transfer across both width and depth?
How many Newton-Schulz steps, and at what precision, are needed as matrices get larger, and is the extra compute worth it?
Why do some recipes prefer WSD and others cosine? The GLM-4.5 underfitting result suggests the answer depends on data and model.
Are compute-optimal token ratios still the right target when inference cost dominates and models are deliberately overtrained?

connects.why: Muon's Newton-Schulz runs in bfloat16 and optimizer state precision interacts with FP8 training; DeepSeek-V4 combines Muon with FP8 and FP4.
Moonlight, Kimi K2, GLM-4.5 and DeepSeek-V4 all apply Muon to MoE models, where per-expert matrices and sharding complicate orthogonalization.
Scaling laws set token budgets, and data quality shifts the compute-optimal ratio between parameters and tokens.
Small models are trained far past Chinchilla-optimal; WSD schedules make that overtraining cheap to plan.

threads.title: Low precision: FP8 and FP4 training and 1.58-bit models
threads.dek: Every halving of bits roughly halves memory traffic and can double matmul throughput. The field went from FP32 to BF16 to FP8, is now pretraining in 4-bit formats, and some models use only three weight values.

sections.heading: Bits are the cheapest speedup
sections.md:
Training and serving a large model is dominated by matrix multiplications and by moving weights and activations through memory. Both scale with the number of bits per number. A 32-bit float (FP32) costs twice the memory and bandwidth of a 16-bit one, and on recent GPUs the tensor cores run 8-bit and 4-bit matmuls at higher peak rates than 16-bit ones.

The catch is numerical. A floating-point number splits its bits between an **exponent** (range: how big or small it can be) and a **mantissa** (precision: how many distinct values in each power of two). Fewer bits means values underflow to zero, overflow, or get rounded so coarsely that gradient updates vanish. Each step down the ladder needed a trick to keep training stable, and the tricks are the story of this thread.

The payoff is concrete. OpenAI's gpt-oss model card reports that quantizing the MoE weights (90 percent of parameters) to MXFP4, at 4.25 bits per parameter, lets the 120B model fit on a single 80GB GPU.

sections.heading: 16 bits: master weights, loss scaling and bfloat16
sections.md:
**Mixed precision training** (Micikevicius et al., Baidu and NVIDIA, 2017) made FP16 work. Weights, activations and gradients are stored in FP16, but an FP32 *master copy* of the weights accumulates updates, because many updates are too small to change an FP16 number. FP16 has a narrow exponent range, so small gradients underflow; **loss scaling** multiplies the loss by a large constant before backpropagation and divides it out afterwards. The paper reports nearly 2x lower memory use.

**bfloat16** (BF16) takes the other trade: 8 exponent bits like FP32 and only 7 mantissa bits. Kalamkar et al. (Intel and Facebook, 2019) showed BF16 training matches FP32 across domains with no hyperparameter changes, because the FP32-sized range removes the need for loss scaling. BF16 with FP32 master weights became the default recipe for LLMs.

sections.heading: 8 bits: E4M3, E5M2 and finer-grained scaling
sections.md:
FP8 is too narrow for one global format. Micikevicius et al. (NVIDIA, Arm and Intel, 2022) proposed two encodings: **E4M3** (4 exponent, 3 mantissa bits) with extended range for weights and activations, and **E5M2** for gradients, which need range more than precision. Each tensor gets a scale factor so its values land inside the representable range. The authors matched 16-bit quality on models up to 175B parameters with unchanged hyperparameters. Microsoft's **FP8-LM** (Peng et al., 2023) extended FP8 to gradients, optimizer states and distributed communication, reporting a 39 percent memory reduction and 75 percent speedup over BF16 Megatron-LM on a 175B model.

Long runs exposed new failures. Fishman et al. (Intel and Technion, 2024) trained in FP8 to 2T tokens and found instabilities only after long training, traced to SwiGLU amplifying outliers; their Smooth-SwiGLU fix trained a 7B model on par with BF16 at up to about 34 percent higher throughput.

**DeepSeek-V3** (December 2024) was the first to validate FP8 training on an extremely large model, per its authors. The key change was granularity: instead of one scale per tensor, activations get a scale per 1x128 tile and weights per 128x128 block, with higher-precision accumulation. That let it use E4M3 everywhere, and the authors note the idea matches microscaling formats.

sections.heading: 4 bits: microscaling, MXFP4 and NVFP4
sections.md:
At 4 bits a float (E2M1) has only a handful of values, so the scale must follow the data closely. The **microscaling (MX)** formats (Rouhani et al., 2023, with authors from Microsoft, AMD, Intel, Meta, NVIDIA and Qualcomm) attach a shared scale to every block of 32 elements. In MXFP4 that scale is a power of two stored in 8 bits (UE8M0). The paper showed the first generative LM training with sub-8-bit weights, activations and gradients at minimal accuracy loss.

NVIDIA's **NVFP4**, supported on Blackwell, refines this: blocks of 16, an E4M3 block scale with real mantissa bits, and a second FP32 scale per tensor. NVIDIA's NVFP4 pretraining paper (2025) adds random Hadamard transforms to spread outliers, 2D block scaling so forward and backward passes see consistent values, stochastic rounding for gradients, and keeps some layers in BF16. They trained a 12B model on 10T tokens in NVFP4 with loss and accuracy comparable to FP8. In an 8B ablation, MXFP4 needed 36 percent more tokens to match NVFP4's loss.

In parallel, **Quartet** (Castro et al., 2025) ran all linear-layer matmuls in MXFP4 on Blackwell kernels and fitted a low-precision scaling law showing where fully FP4 training is compute-optimal.

sections.heading: 1.58 bits: ternary weights with BitNet
sections.md:
A different line asks how few weight values a model needs. Microsoft Research's **BitNet** (Wang et al., 2023) replaced linear layers with `BitLinear`, training 1-bit weights from scratch. **BitNet b1.58** (Ma et al., 2024) allowed three values, {-1, 0, +1}, which is $\log_2 3 \approx 1.58$ bits. Weights are scaled by their mean absolute value and rounded; activations use 8 bits. The authors report matching an FP16 LLaMA-style baseline from 3B parameters, with 3.55x less memory and 2.71x lower latency at 3B. The authors note that matrix multiplication with such weights needs only integer additions, no multiplications.

**BitNet b1.58 2B4T** (April 2025) is the first open native ternary model at 2B parameters, trained on 4T tokens, which the authors report performs on par with full-precision open models of similar size. BitNet models are trained from scratch with quantization in the loop (the original BitNet keeps full-precision latent weights and uses a straight-through estimator for gradients), so they do not save training compute the way FP8 or FP4 matmuls do; the gains are at inference. Whether the approach holds at much larger scale is not yet publicly demonstrated.

sections.heading: Where it is now: FP4 pretraining goes to production
sections.md:
FP8 is standard for large training runs, and 4-bit formats are moving from research into flagship models.

**Nemotron 3 Super** (NVIDIA, April 2026), a 120B-total MoE trained on 25T tokens, is the first model in its family pretrained in NVFP4, with all linear layers in NVFP4 except the final 15 percent of the network and some projections kept in BF16. **Nemotron 3 Ultra** (June 2026), a 550B-total MoE, reused the same recipe on 20T tokens; NVIDIA reports an average relative train loss gap under 0.4 percent against BF16 branches. Moonshot's **Kimi K2 Thinking** (November 2025) shipped INT4 MoE weights learned with QAT. **DeepSeek-V4** (April 2026) applies MXFP4 quantization-aware training to MoE expert weights and to the query-key path of its attention indexer (a small scorer that picks which past tokens each query attends to) during post-training. The authors report that the FP4 weights dequantize losslessly to FP8, since E4M3 has enough extra exponent range to absorb the fine-grained FP4 block scales (a condition they verify), so the existing FP8 training framework is reused unchanged.

Research is now focused on why FP4 training diverges and how to simplify the recipe. A May 2026 study on AMD MI355X GPUs with native MXFP4 found quantizing *weight gradients* is the main cause of divergence, and that deterministic Hadamard rotations fix it where stochastic rounding does not. A July 2026 paper traces instability to forward and backward passes scaling the same values differently after transposition and enforces 2D blocks, reporting stable FP4 training up to a 30B MoE. A September 2026 report pairs FP4 with wider UE5M3 block scales so it can drop Hadamard transforms and BF16 final layers, a simpler recipe with less work outside the FP4 matmuls. These are recent single-group results, mostly at 8B scale or below.

lineage.title: Mixed Precision Training
lineage.contribution: FP16 storage and math with an FP32 master copy of the weights and loss scaling to keep small gradients from underflowing; nearly 2x memory savings.

lineage.title: A Study of BFLOAT16 for Deep Learning Training
lineage.contribution: Showed bfloat16, with FP32's exponent range, matches FP32 training across domains without hyperparameter changes or loss scaling.

lineage.title: LLM.int8(): 8-bit Matrix Multiplication for Transformers at Scale
lineage.contribution: Found that large transformers develop a few outlier feature dimensions that break naive 8-bit quantization, and handled them in 16-bit while the rest runs in int8.

lineage.title: FP8 Formats for Deep Learning
lineage.contribution: Defined E4M3 and E5M2 8-bit floats; matched 16-bit training quality on models up to 175B with unchanged hyperparameters.

lineage.title: BitNet: Scaling 1-bit Transformers for Large Language Models
lineage.who: Wang, Ma, Dong, Huang, Wei et al. (Microsoft Research)
lineage.contribution: BitLinear layers that train binary weights from scratch, competitive with 8-bit quantization and FP16 baselines at much lower memory and energy.

lineage.title: Microscaling Data Formats for Deep Learning
lineage.who: Rouhani et al. (Microsoft, AMD, Intel, Meta, NVIDIA, Qualcomm)
lineage.contribution: Block formats with one shared power-of-two scale per 32 elements (MXFP8, MXFP6, MXFP4, MXINT8); first sub-8-bit training of generative LMs with minimal loss.

lineage.title: FP8-LM: Training FP8 Large Language Models
lineage.contribution: FP8 for gradients, optimizer states and communication; reported 39 percent less memory and 75 percent faster than BF16 Megatron-LM on GPT-175B.

lineage.title: The Era of 1-bit LLMs: All Large Language Models are in 1.58 Bits
lineage.contribution: Ternary weights {-1, 0, +1} via absmean rounding with 8-bit activations; reported matching FP16 LLaMA-style models from 3B with far lower memory and latency.

lineage.title: Scaling FP8 training to trillion-token LLMs
lineage.contribution: FP8 runs to 2T tokens revealed late instabilities from SwiGLU outlier amplification; Smooth-SwiGLU and FP8 Adam moments fixed them on a 7B model.

lineage.title: DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report (FP8 training)
lineage.contribution: Fine-grained FP8 scaling (1x128 activation tiles, 128x128 weight blocks) with higher-precision accumulation, validated on a 671B-parameter MoE; E4M3 for all tensors.

lineage.title: BitNet b1.58 2B4T Technical Report
lineage.contribution: First open native ternary LLM at 2B parameters, trained on 4T tokens, reported on par with similar-size full-precision open models, with GPU and CPU inference code.

lineage.title: Quartet: Native FP4 Training Can Be Optimal for Large Language Models
lineage.who: Castro, Panferov, Tabesh, Sieberling et al.
lineage.contribution: All linear-layer matmuls in MXFP4 with Blackwell kernels, plus a low-precision scaling law showing when fully FP4 training is compute-optimal.

lineage.title: Pretraining Large Language Models with NVFP4
lineage.contribution: NVFP4 (16-element blocks, E4M3 block scales, FP32 tensor scale) plus Hadamard transforms, 2D scaling and stochastic rounding; 12B model on 10T tokens comparable to FP8.

frontier.title: UE5M3 FP4 Block Scaling for Stable Language Model Pretraining
frontier.note: Pairs FP4 payloads with wider unsigned E5M3 block scales so the recipe can drop Hadamard transforms and BF16 final layers. On a Nemotron-H 8B run of about 190B tokens (software emulated) it reports lower loss than the NVFP4 recipe.

frontier.title: Stable FP4 Training via Transposition-Invariant Block Quantization
frontier.note: Traces FP4 instability to forward and backward passes scaling the same values differently after transposition, and fixes it with 2D blocks. Reports stable FP4 training up to a 30B MoE with under 1.3 percent degradation versus BF16.

frontier.title: Nemotron 3 Ultra: NVFP4 pretraining at 550B
frontier.note: A 550B-total, 55B-active hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE pretrained in NVFP4 on 20T tokens with the Nemotron 3 Super recipe. NVIDIA calls it the largest stable NVFP4 training run to its knowledge; BF16 branches from 5T, 10T and 16T checkpoints showed under 0.4 percent average relative train loss gap.

frontier.title: Pretraining LLMs with MXFP4 on Native FP4 Hardware
frontier.who: Cim et al. (Penn State and AMD)
frontier.note: Controlled Llama 3.1-8B study on AMD MI355X: quantizing weight gradients drives divergence; deterministic Hadamard rotations restore stability where stochastic rounding and random rotations fail.

frontier.title: Nemotron 3 Super: pretrained in NVFP4
frontier.note: A 120B-total, 12B-active hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE pretrained on 25T tokens with NVFP4 for linear layers, keeping the final 15 percent of the network and some projections in BF16. Open checkpoints.

frontier.title: DeepSeek-V4: FP4 quantization-aware training
frontier.note: MXFP4 QAT for MoE expert weights and the indexer QK path during post-training. FP4 weights dequantize losslessly to FP8, so the FP8 framework is reused unchanged; quantizing index scores to BF16 gives a reported 2x faster top-k selector.

frontier.title: Kimi K2 Thinking: native INT4 via quantization-aware training
frontier.note: A 1T-parameter open MoE reasoning model whose MoE weights use INT4 weight-only quantization, learned with QAT in post-training. Moonshot reports a roughly 2x generation speedup in low-latency mode and reports all benchmarks at INT4, arguing long reasoning traces make post-hoc quantization lossy.

frontier.title: gpt-oss-120b and gpt-oss-20b model card
frontier.note: Open-weight models shipped with MoE weights in MXFP4 (4.25 bits per parameter) after quantization in post-training, letting the 120B model fit on one 80GB GPU and the 20B model run in 16GB.

open: Can full FP4 pretraining (forward, backward and weight gradients) match BF16 at frontier scale without keeping sensitive layers in higher precision?
Which block-scale design wins: MXFP4's power-of-two scales, NVFP4's E4M3 scales, or wider formats like UE5M3? Hardware support will decide as much as accuracy.
Do ternary (1.58-bit) models keep pace with full precision beyond the 2B to 4B scale where open evidence exists?
How do low-precision formats interact with new optimizers like Muon, whose Newton-Schulz step and update scaling assume certain numerical precision?
What are the right precision scaling laws, trading bits per parameter against parameters and tokens at fixed compute?

connects.why: Optimizer state precision and update size interact with FP8 and FP4; DeepSeek-V4 combines Muon with FP8 and FP4.
Post-training quantization and ternary models are the main inference-time route to smaller, cheaper models.
FP8 KV caches and FP4 expert weights change how many requests fit on one GPU.
Expert weights dominate MoE memory, which is why gpt-oss and DeepSeek-V4 put FP4 there first.

threads.title: Data: mixing, curation, synthetic data and model collapse
threads.dek: The web is huge but mostly unusable, and the good part is running out. How labs learned to filter it, weight it, rewrite it with other models, and when training on model output actually hurts.

sections.heading: Most of the web is not training data
sections.md:
A pretraining corpus starts as a raw web crawl, usually Common Crawl: billions of pages of menus, spam, duplicated boilerplate and machine-generated text, with some genuinely useful writing mixed in. Training on all of it wastes compute on junk; training only on the clean part throws away most of the tokens.

The scale of that trade-off is stark. Meta researchers note that state-of-the-art filtering pipelines often remove up to 99% of the initial scrape ([REWIRE, 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04689)). NVIDIA's Nemotron-CC team pointed out that the best open filtered sets (FineWeb-Edu and DCLM) discard about 90% of the data, which is a problem when a single model like Llama 3.1 is trained for 15 trillion tokens ([Nemotron-CC](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.02595)).

Data choices move results as much as architecture tweaks. The DCLM authors report that a 7B model trained on their filtered set came close to Llama 3 8B on MMLU (64% versus 66%) while using about 6.6x less compute ([DCLM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11794)).

So this research direction asks three questions. **What to keep** (filtering and deduplication), **how much of each kind** (data mixing), and **how to make more** when good text runs out (synthetic data). A fourth question shadows the third: does training on model-written text slowly degrade models, the effect called **model collapse**?

sections.heading: Cleaning the crawl: heuristics, dedup, then learned filters
sections.md:
Early corpora were cleaned with rules. Google's T5 paper built **C4** from Common Crawl with heuristic filters ([Raffel et al., 2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1910.10683)). Facebook's **CCNet** (Wenzek et al., 2019) added a learned signal: deduplicate, identify language with fastText, then keep documents that a language model trained on Wikipedia finds likely. The idea of scoring web text by its resemblance to a trusted reference corpus runs through everything that followed.

EleutherAI's **The Pile** (2020) went the other way, stitching 22 curated sources (papers, code, books) into 825 GiB. Then Lee et al. at Google (2021) showed that **deduplication** matters on its own: C4 contained one 61-word sentence repeated over 60,000 times, and deduplicated training made models emit memorized text ten times less often while needing fewer steps.

Falcon's **RefinedWeb** (Penedo et al., 2023) challenged the belief that curated sources are required: strict exact and fuzzy dedup (explicitly inspired by Lee et al.) plus filtering of web data alone beat models trained on The Pile, and still yielded five trillion tokens.

The next step replaced hand rules with **model-based quality classifiers**. Hugging Face's **FineWeb** (2024) documented every ablation behind a 15T-token set from 96 crawl snapshots, and its FineWeb-Edu subset (1.3T tokens) kept pages a classifier judged educational, which sharply lifted knowledge benchmarks like MMLU. The **DCLM** benchmark (Li et al., 2024) turned curation into a controlled competition over a 240T-token pool and concluded that model-based filtering is the key ingredient. Nemotron-CC (late 2024) then pushed back on over-filtering: an ensemble of classifiers plus rephrasing gave a 6.3T-token set that matched DCLM on MMLU with four times more unique real tokens, which suits long training runs.

sections.heading: Choosing the mix without training the big model
sections.md:
Once data is split into domains (web, code, books, papers), someone has to pick proportions. Trying mixtures at full scale is unaffordable, so the lineage here is about **predicting a good mixture from small runs**.

**DoReMi** (Xie et al., Stanford and Google, 2023) trains a small 280M proxy model with group distributionally robust optimization, which upweights domains where the proxy lags a reference model. The resulting weights, used for an 8B model on The Pile, improved average few-shot accuracy by 6.5 points and reached baseline accuracy with 2.6x fewer steps.

**Data mixing laws** (Ye et al., 2024) fit functional forms that predict loss from mixture proportions, then nest them with ordinary scaling laws so small runs forecast large ones. They report a mixture for a 1B model on RedPajama that matched the default mixture trained 48% longer.

**RegMix** (Liu et al., Sea AI Lab, 2024) simplified this to regression: train 512 tiny 1M-parameter models on random mixtures, fit a regressor, pick the predicted best. It matched or beat DoReMi with about 10% of the compute, and found that generic web text correlated with downstream performance more than "high quality" sources like Wikipedia.

The catch is that a web crawl has no natural domains. **WebOrganizer** (Wettig et al., 2025) built topic and format taxonomies, distilled an LLM's labels into small classifiers, and adapted RegMix to choose domain mixtures. Domain mixing turned out to complement quality filtering rather than replace it. NVIDIA's **CLIMB** (2025) automates the same loop by clustering embeddings and searching mixtures with proxy models.

sections.heading: Synthetic data, and the fear of eating your own output
sections.md:
When filtered human text runs short, the obvious move is to have a model write more. Microsoft's **phi-1** (Gunasekar et al., 2023) trained a 1.3B code model on 6B tokens of textbook-quality web data plus 1B tokens of textbooks and exercises generated by GPT-3.5, and reported 50.6% pass@1 on HumanEval. The lesson was that clean, didactic data can stand in for scale, but generation with a frontier model is costly and its contents are opaque.

**WRAP** (Maini et al., Apple and CMU, 2024) addressed both problems explicitly: instead of inventing content, a small open model (1.8B or 7B) *rephrases* existing web pages in styles such as Wikipedia prose or question and answer. On noisy C4 this sped pretraining up about 3x. Rephrasing keeps the facts grounded in real documents while improving form, and it became the dominant recipe; Nemotron-CC adopted WRAP's Wikipedia-style prompt for its low-quality pages.

The worry came from the other direction. Shumailov et al. (2023, later in *Nature* 2024) showed that training each generation of a model on the previous generation's output makes the tails of the distribution disappear, an irreversible degradation they named **model collapse**. Gerstgrasser et al. (2024) then showed this depends on a quietly pessimistic assumption: that synthetic data *replaces* real data. If generations of synthetic data *accumulate* alongside the original real data, collapse did not occur in their language model experiments, and in a linear model the error stays bounded no matter how many iterations run.

sections.heading: Where it is now: rewriting the web at trillion-token scale
sections.md:
The 2025 to 2026 work treats synthetic data as a core part of the corpus rather than a supplement, and treats collapse as a condition to manage.

**Recycling instead of discarding.** Meta's REWIRE (2025) rewrites documents that filters would have thrown away. Mixing these rewrites with high-quality raw text gave gains of 1.0, 1.3 and 2.5 points across 22 tasks at 1B, 3B and 7B, beat having 2x more web data, and about 82% of the mixed-in text came from otherwise discarded pages. DatologyAI's **BeyondWeb** (2025) scaled rephrasing to trillions of tokens and reports up to 7.7x faster training than open web data, with the honest conclusion that no single trick explains the gains.

**Fully open pipelines.** Ai2's Olmo 3 (December 2025) released the whole data flow: a 9T-token cleaned pool, a roughly 6T-token training mix, trillion-scale global dedup, science PDFs converted to text with olmOCR, and new methods for token-constrained mixing and quality-aware upsampling. FineWeb2 extended the FineWeb pipeline to over 1,000 languages.

**Data-bound scaling.** As compute grows faster than text, the question becomes how to squeeze more from a fixed corpus. Kim, Kotha and colleagues (2026) report that rephrasing plateaus near 1.48x data efficiency at 32 rephrases per document, while stitching rephrases of one document into a single long "megadoc" reaches 1.80x. SynPro (Yu and Xiong, 2026) trains its rephrasers with RL and reports 3.4 to 5.2x the effective tokens of plain repetition, at small scale (up to 2B parameters).

**Collapse, recalibrated.** A 2026 statistical analysis (Bakshi and Chakraborty) shows that keeping some fresh real data can avoid collapse and even recover the target distribution, and an ICML 2026 position paper (Schaeffer et al.) counts eight distinct definitions of model collapse and argues several prominent scenarios rest on unrealistic assumptions.

lineage.title: Exploring the Limits of Transfer Learning with a Unified Text-to-Text Transformer (T5, C4)
lineage.contribution: Introduced the T5 model and the Colossal Clean Crawled Corpus (C4), a Common Crawl extract cleaned with heuristic rules that became a standard baseline corpus.

lineage.title: CCNet: Extracting High Quality Monolingual Datasets from Web Crawl Data
lineage.contribution: Pipeline that deduplicates crawl data, identifies language with fastText, and keeps documents close to high-quality reference text like Wikipedia using a language model score.

lineage.title: The Pile: An 800GB Dataset of Diverse Text for Language Modeling
lineage.contribution: An 825 GiB corpus built from 22 curated subsets (academic, code, books, web), showing that source diversity improves cross-domain generalization. Its domains became the test bed for later mixing methods.

lineage.title: Deduplicating Training Data Makes Language Models Better
lineage.contribution: Exact substring and near-duplicate removal tools. Found one sentence repeated over 60,000 times in C4; deduplicated training cut verbatim memorization tenfold and reached the same accuracy in fewer steps.

lineage.title: DoReMi: Optimizing Data Mixtures Speeds Up Language Model Pretraining
lineage.who: Xie et al., Stanford and Google
lineage.contribution: Learns domain weights with a small proxy model trained by group DRO, then trains a 30x larger model on the reweighted data. On The Pile: +6.5 points few-shot and baseline accuracy in 2.6x fewer steps.

lineage.title: The Curse of Recursion: Training on Generated Data Makes Models Forget
lineage.contribution: Named model collapse: recursively training on model-generated data makes the tails of the original distribution vanish, in VAEs, Gaussian mixtures and LLMs. Published in Nature in 2024.

lineage.title: The RefinedWeb Dataset for Falcon LLM
lineage.who: Penedo et al., Technology Innovation Institute
lineage.contribution: Showed that strictly filtered and deduplicated web data alone can beat curated corpora like The Pile, while still yielding five trillion tokens. Dedup design follows Lee et al.

lineage.title: Textbooks Are All You Need (phi-1)
lineage.contribution: A 1.3B code model trained on 6B tokens of textbook-quality web data plus 1B tokens of GPT-3.5-generated textbooks and exercises, reaching 50.6% on HumanEval and popularizing synthetic pretraining data.

lineage.title: Rephrasing the Web: A Recipe for Compute and Data-Efficient Language Modeling (WRAP)
lineage.who: Maini et al., Apple and CMU
lineage.contribution: Uses a small instruction-tuned model to rephrase web pages in styles like Wikipedia or Q and A, trained jointly with real data. About 3x faster pretraining on C4, and cheaper than phi-style generation.

lineage.title: Data Mixing Laws: Optimizing Data Mixtures by Predicting Language Modeling Performance
lineage.contribution: Fits functions predicting performance from mixture proportions and nests them with step and size scaling laws, so small runs choose mixtures for large ones. Compared against DoReMi.

lineage.title: Is Model Collapse Inevitable? Breaking the Curse of Recursion by Accumulating Real and Synthetic Data
lineage.contribution: Showed collapse comes from replacing real data with synthetic data. Accumulating synthetic generations alongside the original real data avoided collapse empirically, with a bounded-error proof for linear models.

lineage.title: DataComp-LM: In search of the next generation of training sets for language models
lineage.who: Li, Fang et al., DataComp consortium
lineage.contribution: A controlled benchmark for data curation over a 240T-token pool with fixed training recipes. Found model-based filtering key; its 7B baseline came close to Llama 3 8B on MMLU (64% vs 66%) with 6.6x less compute.

lineage.title: The FineWeb Datasets: Decanting the Web for the Finest Text Data at Scale
lineage.contribution: A 15T-token open dataset from 96 crawl snapshots with every design choice ablated, plus FineWeb-Edu, a 1.3T-token subset selected by an educational-quality classifier.

lineage.title: RegMix: Data Mixture as Regression for Language Model Pre-training
lineage.who: Liu et al., Sea AI Lab
lineage.contribution: Trains 512 tiny models on random mixtures and fits a regressor to pick the best one. Matched or beat DoReMi with about 10% of the compute.

lineage.title: Nemotron-CC: Transforming Common Crawl into a Refined Long-Horizon Pretraining Dataset
lineage.contribution: Classifier ensembles, WRAP-style rephrasing and lighter heuristics give 6.3T tokens matching DCLM on MMLU with four times more unique real tokens, suited to 15T-token training runs.

lineage.title: Organize the Web: Constructing Domains Enhances Pre-Training Data Curation
lineage.contribution: Builds topic and format domains for web pages using classifiers distilled from an LLM, then adapts RegMix to choose domain mixtures. Shows domain mixing complements quality filtering.

frontier.title: Position: Multiple Definitions and Unrealistic Assumptions of Model Collapse Distract from Real World Threats
frontier.note: Counts eight distinct, sometimes conflicting definitions of model collapse in the literature and argues that several prominent collapse scenarios rest on assumptions that poorly match how data is actually gathered, and are readily avoidable. First posted to arXiv in March 2025 as "Model Collapse Does Not Mean What You Think".

frontier.title: SynPro: Generating Pretraining Tokens from Organic Data for Data-Bound Scaling
frontier.note: Rephrasing and reformatting generators trained with RL on quality, faithfulness and data-influence rewards, refreshed as pretraining plateaus. The authors report 3.4 to 5.2x the effective tokens of plain repetition, in 400M to 2B models.

frontier.title: Data-efficient pre-training by scaling synthetic megadocs
frontier.note: Simple rephrasing plateaus near 1.48x data efficiency at 32 rephrases per document. Stitching rephrases of one document into a long megadoc, or inserting rationales, reaches 1.80x, and the advantage grows with more generations.

frontier.title: From Collapse to Improvement: Statistical Perspectives on Iterative Training on Contaminated Sources
frontier.note: A theoretical analysis of next-token models trained iteratively on a mix of real and synthetic data: with a non-trivial (even decaying) share of fresh real data and suitable sample sizes, collapse is avoided and the true distribution can be recovered.

frontier.title: Olmo 3 (Dolma 3 data)
frontier.note: Releases the entire data flow: a 9T-token cleaned pretraining pool, a roughly 6T-token mix, trillion-scale global dedup tooling, olmOCR-converted science PDFs, token-constrained mixing and quality-aware upsampling.

frontier.title: BeyondWeb: Lessons from Scaling Synthetic Data for Trillion-scale Pretraining
frontier.note: Rephrasing-based synthetic data at trillion-token scale. Reports up to 7.7x faster training than open web data and a 3B model beating an 8B model trained on Cosmopedia at the same 180B-token budget; stresses that many factors must be tuned jointly.

frontier.title: Recycling the Web (REWIRE)
frontier.note: Rewrites low-quality documents that filters would discard. Mixed with high-quality raw text, it beats training on 2x more web data, and about 82% of the mixed-in text comes from pages that would otherwise be thrown away.

frontier.title: FineWeb2: One Pipeline to Scale Them All
frontier.note: Adapts the FineWeb pipeline automatically to any language, adds rebalancing by duplication count and quality, and releases a 20 TB multilingual dataset covering over 1,000 languages.

open: How far can rephrasing go: is there a ceiling on the effective-token multiplier from rewriting a fixed human corpus, and does it hold at frontier scale?
Which quality signal should filters optimize, given that classifier targets like educational value can quietly narrow topic and style coverage?
Do mixtures chosen with tiny proxy models stay optimal at 100x scale and over trillion-token horizons, or do domain interactions change?
How much model-generated text is already in new web crawls, and can it be detected well enough to keep real data from being crowded out?
When synthetic data comes from a stronger model, how much of the gain is knowledge transfer (distillation) rather than better formatting?

connects.why: Data mixing laws are fitted together with compute scaling laws, and data-bound regimes change how optimal model size and token counts are chosen.
Synthetic data from a stronger model is a form of distillation, the same idea used to train small models from large ones.
Model collapse is the pretraining version of the risk in self-improvement loops: a model learning from its own outputs.
Tokenizers are trained on the pretraining corpus, so filtering and multilingual coverage decisions shape tokenization too.

threads.title: From RLHF to DPO to RL with verifiable rewards
threads.dek: Post-training began by teaching models what people prefer, then learned to skip the reward model, and now trains reasoning against answers a program can check. How each step fixed the last one's cost.

sections.heading: You cannot write a loss function for helpful
sections.md:
A pretrained language model predicts the next token of internet text. That makes it knowledgeable but not aligned with what a user wants: it may continue a question with more questions, invent facts, or produce toxic text, because all of that appears in its training data.

There is no differentiable loss for "a good answer". What you can get cheaply is a *comparison*: shown two answers, a person can usually say which is better. The whole lineage in this thread is about turning such signals into gradient updates, and each step trades off three costs: how much human labeling it needs, how much compute and engineering the optimizer needs, and how easily the model can exploit flaws in the signal.

The payoff was large from the start. OpenAI's InstructGPT paper reported that human labelers preferred outputs of a 1.3B model trained with human feedback over those of the 175B GPT-3, despite 100x fewer parameters ([Ouyang et al., 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155)).

The problem with a learned reward is that it is a proxy. Already in 2019, Ziegler et al. found that their summarizers learned to copy whole sentences, which labelers rated highly; the authors suspected the policy was exploiting the simple heuristics labelers relied on. That tension, between optimizing a signal hard and the signal being wrong, is why the field eventually moved to rewards a program can verify.

sections.heading: RLHF: learn a reward model, then optimize it with PPO
sections.md:
**Learning from comparisons.** Christiano, Leike and colleagues (OpenAI and DeepMind, 2017) trained agents on Atari and simulated robots using human preferences between pairs of short clips. A reward model was fit to the comparisons and the agent was trained against it with RL, needing feedback on under 1% of its interactions and about an hour of human time for new behaviors.

**The optimizer.** PPO (Schulman et al., 2017) became the standard algorithm: it takes several gradient steps on each batch of samples while clipping the update so the policy cannot move too far from the policy that generated the data.

**Moving to language.** Ziegler et al. (2019) applied preference-based reward learning with PPO to GPT-2 style models for stylistic continuation and summarization, with a penalty keeping the policy close to the original model. Stiennon et al. (2020) scaled this to Reddit TL;DR summaries and found that optimizing the learned reward model gave summaries people preferred over the human reference summaries, while optimizing ROUGE did not.

**InstructGPT** (Ouyang et al., 2022) made it a general recipe in three steps: supervised fine-tuning on labeler demonstrations, a reward model trained on labeler rankings of outputs, then PPO against that reward. This is the pipeline usually meant by **RLHF**.

**AI feedback.** Anthropic's Constitutional AI (Bai et al., 2022) replaced human harmlessness labels with a model judging outputs against written principles, then trained a preference model on those AI judgments ("RL from AI Feedback", RLAIF). The structure stayed the same; only the source of labels changed.

sections.heading: DPO: skip the reward model entirely
sections.md:
RLHF with PPO is heavy. It needs a reward model, sampling from the policy during training, a value model for the advantage estimates, and careful tuning to stay stable.

**Direct Preference Optimization** (Rafailov, Sharma, Mitchell et al., Stanford, 2023) observed that the KL-regularized RLHF objective has a closed-form optimal policy. Rearranged, the reward can be written in terms of the policy itself: $r(x,y) = \beta \log \frac{\pi(y|x)}{\pi_{ref}(y|x)}$ plus a term that cancels in comparisons. Plugging that into the Bradley-Terry model (which turns the reward gap between two answers into the probability one is preferred) gives a simple classification loss on preferred and rejected pairs, $-\log \sigma\big(r(x,y_w) - r(x,y_l)\big)$. No reward model, no sampling during training, a few lines of code. The paper's subtitle sums it up: your language model is secretly a reward model.

A family of variants followed, each relaxing one assumption:

- **IPO** (Azar et al., DeepMind, 2023) derived a general objective over pairwise preferences and showed DPO can overfit when preferences are deterministic; IPO swaps in an identity mapping with guarantees.
- **KTO** ([Ethayarajh et al., 2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01306)) needs only a binary "desirable or not" label per output, using a utility model from prospect theory, and reports matching preference-based methods from 1B to 30B.
- **SimPO** (Meng, Xia, Chen, Princeton, 2024) drops the reference model, uses the length-normalized average log probability as the implicit reward, and adds a target margin.

Offline methods like these became standard for chat alignment because they are cheap. Their limit is that they learn from a fixed dataset of answers rather than from the model's own fresh attempts, which matters most when the task is hard reasoning.

sections.heading: Verifiable rewards: GRPO, R1 and the reasoning recipe
sections.md:
For math and code, a reward does not have to be learned: a checker can compare the final answer or run tests. That removes much of the proxy problem, though it only judges the end result.

**Outcome versus process.** DeepMind's Uesato et al. (2022) compared rewarding final answers with rewarding each reasoning step on GSM8K, finding similar final-answer error but far fewer reasoning errors with process-based signals. OpenAI's **Let's Verify Step by Step** (Lightman et al., 2023) trained a **process reward model** (PRM) on 800,000 human step labels (PRM800K) and solved 78% of a MATH subset by using it to pick among samples.

**A cheaper optimizer.** DeepSeekMath (Shao et al., 2024) introduced **GRPO**, a PPO variant that drops the value model: sample a group of answers to the same prompt and use the group's mean reward as the baseline for each answer's advantage. That saves the memory of a second large network.

**Naming RLVR.** Ai2's Tulu 3 (Lambert et al., 2024) called the method **RL with verifiable rewards** (RLVR) and used it in an open post-training recipe alongside SFT and DPO.

**The breakthrough.** DeepSeek-R1 (January 2025) applied GRPO with rule-based rewards directly to a base model. In R1-Zero, AIME 2024 pass@1 rose from 15.6% to 71.0% over training, and long chains of thought with self-checking emerged without any human-written reasoning traces. R1 added a small cold-start dataset and multiple stages to fix readability.

**Open replications.** ByteDance's **DAPO** (2025) published four fixes (decoupled clipping, dynamic sampling, token-level loss, overlong reward shaping) reaching 50 points on AIME 2024 from Qwen2.5-32B base. **Dr. GRPO** (Liu et al., 2025) showed GRPO's normalization biases it toward longer wrong answers and removed that bias.

sections.heading: Where it is now: scaling RL, and arguing about what it teaches
sections.md:
**Stability at scale.** Qwen's GSPO (July 2025) moved importance ratios and clipping from tokens to whole sequences, which the authors report stabilizes RL on mixture-of-experts models and contributed to Qwen3. DeepSeek-V3.2 (December 2025) spent a post-training budget over 10% of pretraining cost and listed GRPO fixes for that scale: an unbiased KL estimate, masking stale off-policy negative samples, and keeping MoE routing consistent between sampling and training. DeepSeek-V4 (April 2026) then trained domain experts with GRPO and merged them by on-policy distillation, where one student learns from the experts' scores on its own samples.

**Predictable RL.** Meta's ScaleRL study (October 2025) ran more than 400,000 GPU-hours of ablations, fit sigmoid compute-performance curves, and found that many popular tweaks change efficiency but not the final ceiling. Their recipe predicted a single run scaled to 100,000 GPU-hours.

**What does RLVR actually add?** Yue et al. (April 2025) found RLVR models win at pass@1 but base models win at large pass@k, suggesting RL mostly sharpens what the base model can already do. Wen et al. (June 2025) disputed this with a metric that also checks the reasoning steps. Shao et al. (June 2025) showed that on Qwen2.5-Math, even random rewards raised MATH-500 by 21.4 points (versus 29.1 with true rewards), via a clipping bias that amplifies pretrained habits, while the effect largely failed on Llama and OLMo. The practical lesson: validate RL claims on more than one model family.

**Beyond checkable answers.** Rubrics as Rewards (Scale AI, July 2025) turns instance-specific rubrics into rewards for medicine and science. RLSVR (July 2026) converts open-ended tasks into games whose outcomes are verifiable by construction, such as a social deduction vote.

DeepSeek-R1 was published in [*Nature*](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41586-025-09422-z) in September 2025, a sign of how quickly verifiable-reward RL became the default recipe for reasoning models.

Can process reward models be made cheap and robust enough to use inside RL at scale, rather than mainly for reranking samples?
Which RL results generalize across model families, given that some gains appear only on particular base models?
What is the right split of compute between pretraining and RL as post-training budgets pass 10% of pretraining?

Every reward here is a proxy that can be gamed, from RLHF reward models to unit tests in coding RL.
Agentic post-training extends RLVR to multi-step tool use, with environments as the verifier.
GSPO and DeepSeek-V3.2's routing fixes exist because RL on MoE models is unstable.

threads.title: Reasoning at test time: thinking longer, and thinking less
threads.dek: Letting a model think before answering became the biggest capability lever since scale. Now the work is about spending those thinking tokens wisely, or moving the thinking out of words entirely.

sections.heading: A fixed amount of compute per token is not enough
sections.md:
A transformer spends roughly the same computation on every token it emits. A one-word answer to a hard math problem therefore gets as much thought as a one-word answer to "what is 2+3". **Test-time compute** is the family of ideas that let a model spend more computation on harder questions at inference time, instead of only making the model bigger.

There are two basic levers. A model can produce more tokens in sequence (a **chain of thought**, where it writes intermediate steps), or it can produce many candidate answers in parallel and pick one (sampling plus voting or a verifier). Reasoning models trained with RL now do the first at large scale: OpenAI reports that gpt-oss-20b uses over 20,000 chain-of-thought tokens per AIME problem on average ([gpt-oss model card, 2025](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.10925)).

That cost is the second half of this story. Long thinking is slow and expensive to serve, and models also think at length about easy questions, which Chen et al. called **overthinking** ([2024](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.21187)). So the field is pulled two ways at once: scale thinking up where it helps, and cut it where it does not.

sections.heading: Thinking in words: chain of thought, voting and search
sections.md:
**Chain of thought.** Wei et al. (Google, January 2022) showed that giving a large model a few worked examples with intermediate steps sharply improves arithmetic, commonsense and symbolic reasoning; a 540B model with eight such exemplars set a new state of the art on GSM8K. Kojima et al. (2022) found that simply appending "Let's think step by step" gets much of the effect with no examples, raising text-davinci-002 on MultiArith from 17.7% to 78.7%.

**Sampling many thoughts.** Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022) samples several reasoning paths and takes a majority vote over final answers, adding 17.9 points on GSM8K over greedy chain of thought. This is the simplest form of parallel test-time compute.

**Searching over thoughts.** Tree of Thoughts (Yao et al., Princeton and Google DeepMind, 2023) treats intermediate steps as nodes, has the model evaluate them, and searches with lookahead and backtracking. On Game of 24, GPT-4 went from 4% with chain of thought to 74%.

**Judging steps.** Search needs a scorer. OpenAI's Let's Verify Step by Step (Lightman et al., 2023) trained a **process reward model** that grades each step, and used it to pick the best of many samples on MATH. These verifiers became the backbone for the next question: how should a fixed inference budget be spent?

sections.heading: Test-time scaling becomes a law, then a training target
sections.md:
**Repeated sampling.** Large Language Monkeys (Brown et al., Stanford and Oxford, 2024) showed that **coverage**, the fraction of problems solved by at least one sample, grows roughly log-linearly over four orders of magnitude of samples. With a checker (unit tests), DeepSeek-Coder-V2 on SWE-bench Lite went from 15.9% with one sample to 56% with 250. Without a checker, majority voting and reward models plateaued after a few hundred samples.

**Compute-optimal inference.** Snell et al. (Berkeley and Google DeepMind, August 2024) compared searching against process verifiers with letting the model revise its own answers, and found the best strategy depends on question difficulty. Allocating compute per prompt was over 4x more efficient than best-of-N, and in FLOPs-matched tests on problems where a small model has some success, extra inference compute beat a 14x larger model.

**Training the model to think.** OpenAI's o1 (September 2024) showed that a model trained with RL to produce long hidden reasoning improves as it is allowed to think longer, without disclosing how. DeepSeek-R1 (January 2025) published a recipe: RL with verifiable rewards on a base model made responses grow longer and develop self-checking on their own.

**The minimal version.** s1 (Muennighoff et al., Stanford and University of Washington, January 2025) fine-tuned Qwen2.5-32B-Instruct on just 1,000 curated reasoning traces and added **budget forcing**: stop the thinking at a token limit, or extend it by appending "Wait" when the model tries to stop. This let AIME 2024 accuracy be pushed from 50% to 57% by thinking longer, and made test-time compute directly controllable.

sections.heading: Thinking less, and thinking without words
sections.md:
Once models were trained to think long, the cost problem arrived. Chen et al. (Tencent, December 2024) measured **overthinking** in o1-like models, defined efficiency metrics for both outcome and process, and showed self-training could shorten reasoning without hurting accuracy. The Stop Overthinking survey (Sui et al., March 2025) sorted the fast-growing field into three families: train models to be concise, cut reasoning dynamically at inference, or shorten via prompting.

**Length control.** L1 (Aggarwal and Welleck, CMU, March 2025) trained with LCPO, an RL objective that rewards both correctness and matching a token budget stated in the prompt. It traded cost against accuracy more smoothly than s1's budget forcing, and its short-reasoning variant beat GPT-4o at equal lengths at 1.5B parameters.

**Latent reasoning.** A different answer is to stop reasoning in tokens. Coconut (Hao et al., Meta, December 2024) feeds the model's last hidden state back as the next input instead of decoding a word. These continuous thoughts can hold several candidate next steps at once, enabling something like breadth-first search, and beat chain of thought on planning-heavy logic tasks.

Geiping et al. (February 2025) instead loop a recurrent block inside the model, so depth, not length, scales at test time; their 3.5B model trained on 800B tokens improved on reasoning benchmarks up to compute equivalent to a 50B model. The **Hierarchical Reasoning Model** (Sapient, June 2025) used two small recurrent modules at different speeds; with 27M parameters and about 1,000 training examples the authors report it solved hard Sudoku and maze tasks and beat much larger models on ARC. An [ARC Prize analysis](https://arcprize.org/blog/hrm-analysis) verified 32% on ARC-AGI-1 but found the hierarchy mattered little; an outer refinement loop drove most of the gain.

The cost of latent reasoning is visibility: a chain of thought in words can be read and monitored, a vector cannot.

sections.heading: Where it is now: effort knobs, inverse scaling and tiny recursive models
sections.md:
**Thinking effort as a product setting.** OpenAI's open-weight gpt-oss (August 2025) was trained with three reasoning levels set in the system prompt ("Reasoning: low"), with accuracy rising smoothly with chain-of-thought length. Moonshot's Kimi K2.5 report (February 2026) describes Toggle, an RL heuristic that alternates between phases that enforce a per-problem token budget and phases that do not, so the model does not lose the ability to think long. Applied to K2 Thinking, the report says it cut output tokens by 25 to 30% on average with negligible accuracy loss.

**Parallel thinking.** Google DeepMind's gold-medal IMO 2025 result used Gemini Deep Think, which explores and combines several candidate solutions in parallel before answering.

**More thinking can hurt.** Gema et al. (July 2025) built tasks where longer reasoning lowers accuracy, with failure modes including distraction by irrelevant details and drift toward spurious correlations. A 2026 study (Zhou et al.) found diminishing returns at high budgets, with models abandoning previously correct answers, and that the best length varies with difficulty.

**Contested limits.** Apple's Illusion of Thinking (June 2025) reported that reasoning models collapse on puzzles past a complexity threshold and even reduce effort. A rebuttal by Lawsen argued much of this came from output token limits and unsolvable puzzle instances. Treat claims of hard reasoning ceilings with care.

**Can we trust the words?** Anthropic's Chen et al. (May 2025) found reasoning models often fail to mention hints they actually used; reveal rates were often below 20%. Visible thinking is useful for monitoring but not a faithful transcript.

**Small and recursive.** The Tiny Recursive Model (Jolicoeur-Martineau, Samsung SAIL Montreal, October 2025) simplified HRM to one 2-layer, 7M-parameter network that refines its answer recursively, reporting 45% on ARC-AGI-1. Latent Recurrent Thoughts (September 2026) attaches a small recurrent reasoner to a frozen LLM, which decodes the refined latent thoughts into an answer.

open: How can a model know in advance how hard a problem is, so it spends the right amount of thinking without a human-set budget?
Does latent reasoning scale to general language tasks, or mainly to puzzles with crisp answers?
If reasoning moves into vectors, what replaces reading the chain of thought for monitoring and debugging?

Recurrent-depth and looped models scale computation by depth rather than tokens, the same idea as latent reasoning here.
Long reasoning traces dominate serving cost through KV cache size and decode time.
Chain-of-thought faithfulness and monitoring depend on whether the written reasoning reflects what the model computes.
Routing easy queries to cheap non-thinking paths is the system-level answer to overthinking.
