threads.title: Retrieval: dense, late interaction, learned sparse and fast vector search
threads.dek: How search went from counting words to comparing learned vectors, why one vector per document is not enough, and how graphs and bit tricks made billion-vector search cheap enough to sit under RAG and agent memory.

sections.heading: Finding the right passage among a billion
sections.md:
Every retrieval system answers the same question: given a query, which few items out of a huge collection are relevant? For decades the default answer was **BM25**, a scoring formula over word counts that rewards documents containing the query's rare words. It is fast because it runs on an *inverted index* (a map from each word to the documents containing it), but it only matches words, not meaning. A question about "heart attack" will miss a passage about "myocardial infarction".

The obvious fix is to let a neural network read both query and document and judge relevance. That works, but it is far too slow to run against millions of documents per query. So the field split the problem into a cheap first stage that narrows millions of candidates to a few hundred, and an expensive second stage that reranks them.

This thread is about that first stage, and it has three moving parts. What to store per document (one vector, many vectors, or a sparse bag of weighted words). How to find the nearest stored vectors fast (approximate nearest neighbor search, or **ANN**, which trades a little recall for orders of magnitude of speed). And how to shrink the vectors so billions fit in memory. Once retrieval worked, it also became the memory of LLM systems: RAG, GraphRAG and agent memory are all retrieval with a generator on top.

sections.heading: From word counts to learned vectors, and why one vector is not enough
sections.md:
In 2020, Karpukhin and colleagues at Facebook AI showed with [DPR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.04906) that retrieval could run on dense vectors alone. Two BERT encoders, one for questions and one for passages, are trained so that relevant pairs have a high dot product. Passages are embedded offline and indexed with FAISS. The paper reports that DPR beats a strong Lucene BM25 system by 9 to 19 points of top-20 passage accuracy across open-domain QA datasets.

A single vector per passage is a bottleneck, though: everything the passage says must be squeezed into one point. In the same month Omar Khattab and Matei Zaharia proposed [ColBERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2004.12832), which keeps one vector per token. A query is scored against a document with **late interaction**: for each query token, take its maximum similarity to any document token (*MaxSim*), then sum. Documents are still encoded offline, so this is far cheaper than a cross-encoder, but it stores roughly one vector per token. [ColBERTv2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.01488) (2021) attacked that cost with residual compression and better supervision, cutting the space footprint 6 to 10 times.

A third path kept the inverted index. [SPLADE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.05720) (Formal, Piwowarski and Clinchant, Naver Labs, 2021) uses a BERT model to predict a weight for every vocabulary word, including words that are not in the text (*expansion*), with a regularizer that forces most weights to zero. The output is a sparse vector that classic search engines can serve, but with learned term importance.

Late interaction then jumped to images. [ColPali](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.01449) (2024) skips OCR and layout parsing entirely: a vision-language model embeds patches of the page image into many vectors and scores them with ColBERT-style MaxSim. Google's [MUVERA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.19504) (2024) went the other way and compressed a multi-vector set into one *fixed dimensional encoding* whose inner product approximates MaxSim, so ordinary single-vector indexes can serve multi-vector models.

sections.heading: Graphs, disks, GPUs and bits: making nearest-neighbor search fast
sections.md:
Exact search compares the query to every stored vector: hopeless at a billion. Two ANN families dominate. *Partition and compress* methods cluster the vectors and store each one as a short code; product quantization (PQ, Jegou, Douze and Schmid, 2011) splits a vector into chunks and replaces each chunk by the id of its nearest centroid. FAISS ([Johnson, Douze and Jegou, 2017](https://arxiv.org/abs/1702.08734)) brought these methods to GPUs at billion scale.

*Graph* methods connect each vector to near neighbors and answer a query by greedy walking. [HNSW](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09320) (Malkov and Yashunin, 2016) stacks graphs in layers like a skip list: each element's top layer is drawn with exponentially decaying probability, so search makes long hops on a sparse top layer, then refines downward, scaling roughly logarithmically. HNSW became a vector-database default, but wants everything in RAM.

[DiskANN](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2019/hash/09853c7fb1d3f8ee67a61b6bf4a7f8e6-Abstract.html) (Microsoft Research and collaborators, 2019) moved the graph to SSD. Its Vamana graph keeps long-range edges so few disk reads are needed, and only PQ-compressed vectors are cached in memory. The paper reports a billion-point index on a workstation with 64GB RAM serving over 5,000 queries per second at under 3 ms mean latency and 95%+ 1-recall@1. NVIDIA's [CAGRA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.15136) (2023) built a GPU-native graph and reports 33 to 77 times the large-batch throughput of HNSW at 90 to 95% recall.

Compression got theory with [RaBitQ](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.12497) (Gao and Long, NTU, 2024). It snaps each vector to a randomly rotated hypercube codebook, one bit per dimension, and estimates distances with bit operations. Unlike PQ it comes with a provable error bound, and the authors note PQ variants can fail badly on some real datasets. Real applications also add filters ("only 2024 documents"). [ACORN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.04871) (Stanford, 2024) extends HNSW with a denser graph and *predicate subgraph traversal*, searching only through nodes that pass the filter, and reports 2 to 1,000 times higher throughput than prior methods at fixed recall.

sections.heading: Retrieval becomes memory: RAG, GraphRAG and agents
sections.md:
[RAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.11401) (Lewis et al., Facebook AI, 2020) attached a DPR retriever over a dense Wikipedia index to a BART generator and trained them together, treating retrieved passages as latent variables. The model looks facts up instead of storing them all in weights. Today "RAG" mostly means the simpler pipeline: chunk documents, embed, retrieve top-k, paste into the prompt.

That pipeline fails on questions about a whole corpus, such as "what are the main themes?", because no single chunk holds the answer. Microsoft's [GraphRAG](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16130) (2024) has an LLM extract an entity graph, group related entities into communities, and pre-write a summary per community. A global question is answered map-reduce style over those summaries. The authors report better comprehensiveness and diversity than plain RAG on sensemaking questions over corpora around 1 million tokens.

Agents need memory that is also written to. [MemGPT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.08560) (UC Berkeley, 2023) borrowed the operating system's memory hierarchy: a small main context and larger external stores, with the model itself calling functions to page information in and out. Later systems such as [Mem0](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.19413) (2025) extract, consolidate and update discrete facts from conversations, optionally as a graph; the authors report a 26% relative gain over OpenAI's memory on an LLM-as-judge metric on the LOCOMO benchmark.

sections.heading: Where it is now: one-vector limits, cheaper multi-vector, memory as workload
sections.md:
Four trends dominate the last eighteen months.

**Single vectors have a ceiling.** Google DeepMind's [LIMIT paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.21038) (2025) connects a learning-theory result to retrieval: the number of distinct top-k document sets an embedding can return is bounded by its dimension. Even embeddings optimized directly on the test set hit it, and strong models fail their simple LIMIT dataset. That strengthens the case for multi-vector and sparse models.

**Multi-vector is getting cheap.** A late-interaction page can carry around 1,000 vectors. [EigenLI](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.07561) (2026) finds that a document's token vectors lie near a low-dimensional subspace and keeps only its main eigendirections. With 32 or fewer vectors it beats clustering-based pooling on two of the three text models tested, and its single-vector form beats MUVERA. [GLIE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2609.11808) (2026) observes that visual-document vectors sit on the unit sphere near a manifold of dimension five to six; it indexes 4 learned vectors per page and regenerates the full set only for top candidates; the authors report keeping nearly 80% of uncompressed nDCG@5 on ViDoRe v1.

**Indexes and engines.** [QuIVer](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.02171) (2026) builds the graph itself in a 2-bit space and maps where that works: well on cosine contrastive embeddings, poorly on Euclidean-native data. On the multimodal side, Google's [Gemini Embedding 2](https://blog.google/innovation-and-ai/models-and-research/gemini-models/gemini-embedding-2/) (preview, 2026) maps text, images, video, audio and PDFs into one single-vector space. A [filtered-search study](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.11443) (2026) of FAISS, Milvus and pgvector finds engine behavior often outweighs the index, for example pgvector's planner choosing approximate scans when exact ones would give perfect recall at similar latency.

**Memory as a systems workload.** A [2026 characterization](https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.06448) of ten agent memory systems splits cost into construction, retrieval and generation and finds design choices shift cost between write and read paths.

sections.heading: How it is used in production
sections.md:
A typical modern stack is hybrid. A sparse retriever (BM25 or SPLADE-style) and a dense one run in parallel, their candidate lists are merged, and a cross-encoder or LLM reranks the top few dozen. The dense side lives in an HNSW or DiskANN-style index, usually with compressed vectors (PQ or binary codes) for the first pass and full-precision vectors for a final rescoring.

For visually rich documents (slides, scanned reports, tables) ColPali-style models remove the brittle OCR pipeline, and the cost question becomes how many vectors per page to keep. For agents, retrieval is wrapped in write policies: what to extract, when to merge or forget, and when to rebuild summaries. Those choices, not the ANN index, now drive most of the latency and cost.

lineage.title: Product quantization for nearest neighbor search
lineage.who: Herve Jegou, Matthijs Douze, Cordelia Schmid (INRIA)
lineage.contribution: Splits each vector into sub-vectors and quantizes each against its own small codebook, so a vector becomes a short code and distances to a query are estimated from its codes. Combined with an inverted file, it was validated on two billion vectors.

lineage.title: Hierarchical Navigable Small World graphs (HNSW)
lineage.contribution: A multi-layer proximity graph where each element's top layer is chosen with exponentially decaying probability, so search hops coarse-to-fine like a skip list with roughly logarithmic scaling. Widely adopted as an ANN index in vector databases.

lineage.title: Billion-scale similarity search with GPUs (FAISS)
lineage.who: Jeff Johnson, Matthijs Douze, Herve Jegou (Facebook AI)
lineage.contribution: GPU implementations of exact and compressed-domain (product quantization) search at billion scale, released as the FAISS library that DPR and ColBERT later used for indexing.

lineage.title: DiskANN: billion-point nearest neighbor search on a single node
lineage.who: Suhas Jayaram Subramanya, Harsha Simhadri et al. (Microsoft Research)
lineage.contribution: Vamana graph stored on SSD with PQ-compressed vectors cached in RAM, serving a billion points from one 64GB machine at high recall and millisecond latency. Compared directly against HNSW and NSG.

lineage.title: Dense Passage Retrieval for Open-Domain Question Answering
lineage.contribution: Two BERT encoders trained contrastively so question and passage vectors meet by dot product; indexed with FAISS. Beat Lucene BM25 by 9 to 19 points of top-20 accuracy.

lineage.title: ColBERT: contextualized late interaction over BERT
lineage.contribution: One vector per token, scored by late interaction (sum over query tokens of max similarity to any document token). Keeps documents precomputable while recovering much of a cross-encoder's precision; end-to-end retrieval via faiss.

lineage.title: Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks
lineage.who: Patrick Lewis et al. (Facebook AI, UCL, NYU)
lineage.contribution: Joined a DPR retriever over a dense Wikipedia index with a BART generator, trained end to end with retrieved passages as latent variables. Named the RAG pattern.

lineage.title: SPLADE: Sparse Lexical and Expansion Model
lineage.who: Thibault Formal, Benjamin Piwowarski, Stephane Clinchant (Naver Labs Europe)
lineage.contribution: BERT predicts a weight for every vocabulary term, including expansion terms absent from the text, with a sparsity regularizer and log saturation, so learned representations run on ordinary inverted indexes.

lineage.title: ColBERTv2: lightweight late interaction
lineage.who: Keshav Santhanam, Omar Khattab et al. (Stanford)
lineage.contribution: Residual compression of token vectors plus denoised supervision, improving quality while cutting late interaction's storage 6 to 10 times.

lineage.title: CAGRA: highly parallel graph construction and ANN search for GPUs
lineage.contribution: A proximity graph designed for GPU parallelism. Reports 2.2 to 27 times faster construction and 33 to 77 times higher large-batch throughput than HNSW at 90 to 95% recall.

lineage.title: MemGPT: Towards LLMs as Operating Systems
lineage.contribution: Virtual context management: the LLM pages information between a small main context and external stores using function calls, borrowing the OS memory hierarchy for long chats and documents.

lineage.title: ACORN: predicate-agnostic hybrid search over vectors and structured data
lineage.who: Liana Patel, Peter Kraft, Carlos Guestrin, Matei Zaharia
lineage.contribution: Extends HNSW with a denser graph and predicate subgraph traversal, so filtered queries walk only through nodes that pass the filter. Reports 2 to 1,000 times higher throughput at fixed recall.

lineage.title: From Local to Global: A Graph RAG Approach to Query-Focused Summarization
lineage.contribution: An LLM builds an entity graph and per-community summaries ahead of time, then answers corpus-wide questions map-reduce style over the summaries, where plain chunk RAG fails.

lineage.title: RaBitQ: quantizing high-dimensional vectors with a theoretical error bound
lineage.contribution: Quantizes each vector to a randomly rotated hypercube vertex, one bit per dimension, estimating distances with bitwise or SIMD operations. Unlike PQ, comes with a sharp error bound and outperforms PQ variants on the accuracy-efficiency trade-off.

lineage.title: MUVERA: Multi-Vector Retrieval via Fixed Dimensional Encodings
lineage.contribution: Turns a set of token vectors into one fixed-length vector whose inner product provably approximates multi-vector similarity, so ColBERT-style models can use standard single-vector indexes.

lineage.title: ColPali: Efficient Document Retrieval with Vision Language Models
lineage.contribution: Embeds page images directly with a vision-language model into multi-vector patch embeddings scored by ColBERT-style late interaction, replacing OCR pipelines; introduced the ViDoRe benchmark.

frontier.title: GLIE: Generative Late-Interaction Embeddings for Visual Document Retrieval
frontier.note: Finds visual late-interaction vectors lie on the unit sphere near a 5 to 6 dimensional manifold. Indexes a few learned vectors per page and decodes the full set only for top candidates; at 4 vectors per page keeps nearly 80% of uncompressed nDCG@5 on ViDoRe v1, versus 70% for the best prior post-hoc method.

frontier.title: EigenLI: Spectral Approximations to Late Interaction
frontier.who: Archish S, Ravishankar Krishnaswamy et al.
frontier.note: Compresses each document's token vectors onto its dominant eigendirections. Beats k-means and Ward pooling at 32 or fewer vectors on ColBERTv2 and AnswerAI-ColBERT-small (not on GTE-ModernColBERT), and a single-vector variant beats MUVERA.

frontier.title: Agent Memory: Characterization and System Implications of Stateful Long-Horizon Workloads
frontier.note: Presented by the authors as the first systems characterization of agent memory: profiles ten designs, from flat retrieval to consolidating fact stores, attributing cost to construction, retrieval and generation. Shows design choices move cost between write and read paths and derives ten deployment recommendations.

frontier.title: QuIVer: Rethinking ANN Graph Topology via Training-Free Binary Quantization
frontier.who: Wenxuan Xiao, Zhiyou Wang, Chengcheng Li
frontier.note: Builds and searches a Vamana-style graph entirely on 2-bit codes, using float vectors only to rerank. The authors report at least 88% Recall@10 (ef=64) on cosine-native contrastive embeddings, 71 to 78% on CLIP data and under 15% on Euclidean-native data, mapping where aggressive compression stops working.

frontier.title: Gemini Embedding 2
frontier.note: Google describes it as its first natively multimodal embedding model: text (up to 8192 tokens), images, video up to 120 seconds, audio without transcription and PDFs map into one embedding space, with interleaved inputs and Matryoshka dimensions from 3072 down. Released as a public preview; quality claims are Google's own.

frontier.title: Filtered ANN Search in Vector Databases: System Design and Performance Analysis
frontier.who: Abylay Amanbayev, Brian Tsan, Tri Dang, Florin Rusu
frontier.note: Benchmarks filtering strategies inside FAISS, Milvus and pgvector on a new relational dataset. Finds engine behavior often outweighs raw index quality, such as pgvector picking approximate scans where exact scans would give perfect recall at similar latency.

frontier.title: On the Theoretical Limitations of Embedding-Based Retrieval (LIMIT)
frontier.note: Links the embedding dimension to how many distinct top-k result sets a single-vector model can ever return, shows the limit binds even for vectors optimized on the test set, and releases a simple dataset that strong embedding models fail.

open: Can multi-vector models be stored at close to single-vector cost without losing the precision that made them worth using?
If single-vector embeddings have a dimension-bound ceiling, what should replace them for instruction-following and reasoning-heavy retrieval?
How should filters, freshness and deletions be handled inside ANN indexes without rebuilding graphs or losing recall?
What should an agent write to memory, when should it merge or forget, and how do we evaluate that over months rather than one benchmark?
When does building a graph index (GraphRAG) pay back its LLM extraction cost compared with long-context models reading raw text?

connects.why: Agent long-term memory is retrieval with a write path; memory design shapes what tools and plans an agent can use.
ColPali and CLIP-style encoders come from vision-language models; retrieval over images and pages rides on them.
RAG and memory shift cost into prefill; long retrieved contexts interact with KV cache reuse and batching.
Semantic caches and prompt routing reuse the same embedding and ANN machinery.
Vector quantization (PQ, RaBitQ, binary codes) shares ideas and trade-offs with weight and activation quantization.

threads.title: Generative models: diffusion, flow matching and one-step generation
threads.dek: Diffusion models learned to turn noise into images by undoing noise one small step at a time. A decade later the race is to get the same quality in one step, and to drop the latent autoencoder too.

sections.heading: Turning noise into data, one small step at a time
sections.md:
A generative model has to produce new samples (images, audio, video) that look like they came from the training data. Before 2020 the leading approaches were GANs, which train a generator against a discriminator and are fast to sample but unstable to train and prone to dropping parts of the data distribution, and autoregressive models, which are stable but generate one pixel or token at a time.

Diffusion models take a third route. Corrupt a data point with a little Gaussian noise, then a little more, until nothing but noise is left. That *forward process* needs no learning. Then train a network to undo one small step of it. Each step is an easy regression problem, so training is as stable as supervised learning, and chaining many steps turns pure noise into a sample.

The cost is at sampling time: the original models needed hundreds to a thousand network evaluations per image. Much of the story since has been about cutting that number, first to tens, then to a handful, and now to one, without losing quality. The other half of the story is *where* the denoising happens: in pixels, or in the compressed latent space of an autoencoder.

sections.heading: Denoising and scores: DDPM, score matching and the SDE view
sections.md:
The idea dates to [Sohl-Dickstein et al. (2015)](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.03585), who borrowed from non-equilibrium physics: slowly destroy structure with a forward diffusion, then learn the reverse. It worked but did not produce competitive images.

Two lines revived it. Yang Song and Stefano Ermon ([2019](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.05600)) trained a network to estimate the **score**, the gradient of log probability $\nabla_x \log p(x)$, at many noise levels, then sampled by walking uphill with annealed Langevin dynamics. Jonathan Ho, Ajay Jain and Pieter Abbeel's [DDPM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11239) (2020) showed that a simple weighted training objective, predicting the noise that was added, connects diffusion to denoising score matching. DDPM reached an FID of 3.17 on CIFAR-10 (FID measures distance between generated and real image statistics; lower is better).

[Score-based SDEs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.13456) (Song et al., 2020) unified the two: the forward process is a stochastic differential equation, and the reverse-time equation depends only on the score. The same paper described a deterministic *probability flow ODE* with the same marginals, which later became the target for fast samplers. [DDIM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.02502) (Song, Meng and Ermon, 2020) had already shown a non-Markovian sampler with the same training objective could be 10 to 50 times faster in wall-clock time.

Two practical pieces made diffusion dominant. [Classifier-free guidance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.12598) (Ho and Salimans, 2022) trains one model both with and without the condition and extrapolates between the two predictions, trading diversity for prompt adherence with no separate classifier. [Latent diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.10752) (Rombach et al., 2021) ran diffusion inside the latent space of a pretrained autoencoder instead of pixels, cutting the hundreds of GPU days pixel models needed, and added cross-attention for text conditioning. It became Stable Diffusion.

sections.heading: Straight paths: flow matching, rectified flow and transformers
sections.md:
In 2022 three groups independently reframed generation as learning a velocity field that transports noise to data along a chosen path. [Flow matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.02747) (Lipman et al., Meta) regresses the network onto the velocity of simple per-sample conditional paths, which avoids simulating the ODE during training; diffusion paths are a special case, and straight optimal-transport paths train and sample faster. [Rectified flow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.03003) (Liu, Gong and Liu) uses straight lines between noise and data, and *reflow* repeatedly retrains on the model's own pairings to straighten the paths further, so a coarse solver needs fewer steps. [Stochastic interpolants](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.15571) (Albergo and Vanden-Eijnden) arrived at the same quadratic velocity loss.

The training objective is almost trivial. With noise $x_0$, data $x_1$ and $x_t = (1-t)x_0 + t x_1$, the network $v_\theta(x_t, t)$ is trained to predict $x_1 - x_0$.

The backbone changed at the same time. [DiT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09748) (Peebles and Xie, 2022) replaced the U-Net with a plain transformer over latent patches and showed quality improves steadily with compute, reaching FID 2.27 on ImageNet 256. Stability AI's [Stable Diffusion 3 paper](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.03206) (Esser et al., 2024) combined the two: rectified flow trained with noise levels biased toward perceptually important scales, and an MM-DiT that builds on DiT with separate weights for text and image tokens. Rectified-flow transformers are now the common recipe for large image and video models.

A second idea from this period matters for what follows. [REPA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.06940) (Yu et al., 2024) aligned a diffusion transformer's hidden states to features from a pretrained self-supervised encoder such as DINOv2, and the authors report over 17.5 times faster training of SiT models. The authors argue that learning good representations, not just denoising, is a main bottleneck in training diffusion transformers.

sections.heading: Fewer steps: distillation, consistency and mean flows
sections.md:
The first route to fewer steps was *distillation*: train a student to imitate several teacher steps at once. [Progressive distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.00512) (Salimans and Ho, 2022) halves the step count of a DDIM sampler, then repeats. [Adversarial diffusion distillation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.17042) (Stability AI, 2023) added a GAN-style loss and gave 1 to 4 step samplers for SDXL. Distillation works, but needs a trained teacher and a second, often fragile, training stage.

[Consistency models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.01469) (Song, Dhariwal, Chen and Sutskever, OpenAI, 2023) asked for a network that maps *any* point on a probability-flow trajectory straight to its endpoint. That allows one-step sampling by design, and can be trained by distillation or from scratch; the paper reports one-step FID 3.55 on CIFAR-10. Training was unstable at scale until [sCM](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.11081) (Lu and Song, 2024) diagnosed the causes in continuous time and scaled to 1.5B parameters, reporting 2-step FID 1.88 on ImageNet 512.

A cleaner framing came from flow matching. [Shortcut models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.12557) (Frans et al., Berkeley, 2024) condition the network on the step size as well as the time, so one network can take big or small jumps and needs only one training phase. [MeanFlow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.13447) (Zhengyang Geng, Mingyang Deng, Xingjian Bai, J. Zico Kolter and Kaiming He, CMU and MIT, 2025) models the **average velocity** over an interval rather than the instantaneous one, and derives an identity linking the two that gives a training target with no teacher, no distillation and no curriculum. It reported a one-step FID of 3.43 on ImageNet 256 trained from scratch, which became the reference point for the next wave.

sections.heading: Where it is now: one step, no latents, new objectives
sections.md:
Since late 2025 the frontier has moved on three fronts.

**One-step quality has nearly closed the gap.** [Improved MeanFlow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.02012) (Zhengyang Geng et al. with Kaiming He, December 2025) recast the MeanFlow loss as a regression on instantaneous velocity and made guidance a conditioning input, reporting 1-NFE FID 1.72 on ImageNet 256 from scratch. [Drifting models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.04770) (Mingyang Deng et al. with Kaiming He, February 2026) leave diffusion behind: a *drifting field* moves the generator's output distribution during training until it matches the data, so inference is one pass (FID 1.54 latent, 1.61 pixel). [W-Flow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.11755) (May 2026) compresses an optimal-transport gradient flow from noise to data into a one-step generator (FID 1.29), and [Priming Models](https://arxiv.org/abs/2610.20331) (October 2026) pretrain on plain pixel denoising, then post-train with a feature-space distributional loss (FID 1.19, about a tenth of the compute). Setups differ, so these numbers are not directly comparable.

**The autoencoder is being questioned.** [RAE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.11690) (Zheng et al. with Saining Xie, October 2025) replaces the usual VAE with a frozen representation encoder (DINO, SigLIP or MAE) plus a trained decoder, and converges faster without REPA-style alignment losses. [JiT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.13720) (Tianhong Li and Kaiming He, MIT, November 2025) argues networks should predict the clean image, which lies on a low-dimensional manifold, not noise, so plain large-patch transformers work on raw pixels. [Pixel MeanFlow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2601.22158) (Yiyang Lu et al., January 2026) combines that idea with MeanFlow for one-step, latent-free generation at FID 2.22 on ImageNet 256.

**Video and production.** [AnyFlow](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.13724) (May 2026) distills video models into *flow maps* over arbitrary intervals, so one model works at any step count. [Perceptual Flow Matching](https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.03524) (July 2026) supervises flow matching in a pretrained perceptual feature space and reports 4 to 8 steps instead of 35 to 50, with no teacher.

lineage.title: Deep Unsupervised Learning using Nonequilibrium Thermodynamics
lineage.contribution: Introduced the diffusion recipe: destroy structure with a fixed iterative forward noising process, then learn the reverse process as a tractable generative model.

lineage.title: Generative Modeling by Estimating Gradients of the Data Distribution
lineage.contribution: Learned the score (gradient of log density) at many noise levels and sampled with annealed Langevin dynamics, giving GAN-competitive samples without adversarial training.

lineage.title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM)
lineage.who: Jonathan Ho, Ajay Jain, Pieter Abbeel (UC Berkeley)
lineage.contribution: A simple noise-prediction objective that connects diffusion models to denoising score matching; first diffusion model with state-of-the-art image quality (FID 3.17 on CIFAR-10).

lineage.title: Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models (DDIM)
lineage.who: Jiaming Song, Chenlin Meng, Stefano Ermon
lineage.contribution: Non-Markovian sampling with the same training objective as DDPM, giving deterministic samplers 10 to 50 times faster in wall-clock time.

lineage.title: Score-Based Generative Modeling through Stochastic Differential Equations
lineage.contribution: Unified score models and diffusion as forward and reverse-time SDEs whose reverse depends only on the score, and introduced the deterministic probability flow ODE used by later fast samplers.

lineage.title: High-Resolution Image Synthesis with Latent Diffusion Models
lineage.who: Robin Rombach, Andreas Blattmann, Dominik Lorenz, Patrick Esser, Bjorn Ommer
lineage.contribution: Ran diffusion in the latent space of a pretrained autoencoder and added cross-attention conditioning, making high-resolution text-to-image affordable; the basis of Stable Diffusion.

lineage.title: Progressive Distillation for Fast Sampling of Diffusion Models
lineage.contribution: Repeatedly distills a deterministic sampler into a student that takes half as many steps, plus parameterizations that stay stable at few steps.

lineage.title: Classifier-Free Diffusion Guidance
lineage.contribution: Trains one model with and without the condition and extrapolates between their predictions, trading diversity for fidelity without a separate classifier. Standard in text-to-image systems.

lineage.title: Flow Straight and Fast: Learning to Generate and Transfer Data with Rectified Flow
lineage.who: Xingchao Liu, Chengyue Gong, Qiang Liu (UT Austin)
lineage.contribution: Learns an ODE that follows straight lines between noise and data; repeated rectification (reflow) straightens paths so coarse solvers need few steps.

lineage.title: Flow Matching for Generative Modeling
lineage.who: Yaron Lipman et al. (Meta AI, Weizmann)
lineage.contribution: Simulation-free training of continuous normalizing flows by regressing velocities of fixed conditional paths; diffusion paths are a special case and optimal-transport paths train and sample faster.

lineage.title: Scalable Diffusion Models with Transformers (DiT)
lineage.contribution: Replaced the U-Net in latent diffusion with a transformer over latent patches and showed quality improves steadily with compute; FID 2.27 on ImageNet 256.

lineage.title: Consistency Models
lineage.who: Yang Song, Prafulla Dhariwal, Mark Chen, Ilya Sutskever (OpenAI)
lineage.contribution: A network that maps any point on a probability-flow trajectory directly to its endpoint, giving one-step generation by design, trainable by distillation or from scratch.

lineage.title: Scaling Rectified Flow Transformers for High-Resolution Image Synthesis (SD3)
lineage.contribution: Rectified flow with noise sampling biased to perceptually relevant scales, and MM-DiT, a DiT variant with separate text and image weights; showed predictable scaling for text-to-image.

lineage.title: Simplifying, Stabilizing and Scaling Continuous-Time Consistency Models (sCM)
lineage.contribution: Identified the causes of continuous-time consistency training instability and fixed them, scaling to 1.5B parameters with 2-step FID 1.88 on ImageNet 512.

lineage.title: One Step Diffusion via Shortcut Models
lineage.who: Kevin Frans, Danijar Hafner, Sergey Levine, Pieter Abbeel
lineage.contribution: Conditions a flow model on step size as well as time, so one network trained in one phase can sample in one or many steps.

lineage.title: Mean Flows for One-step Generative Modeling
lineage.who: Zhengyang Geng, Mingyang Deng, Xingjian Bai, J. Zico Kolter, Kaiming He
lineage.contribution: Models average velocity over an interval and trains via an identity linking it to instantaneous velocity, with no teacher or curriculum; one-step FID 3.43 on ImageNet 256 from scratch.

frontier.title: Are We Overthinking One-Step Generation? (Priming Models)
frontier.who: Woobin Park, Jaeyeon Kim, Yilun Du, Sitan Chen, Bohyung Han (SNU, Harvard)
frontier.note: A two-stage recipe: train on a reconstruction objective (pixel denoising at one fixed noise level), then post-train with a feature-space distributional loss. The authors report one-step FID 1.19 on ImageNet 256 with about a tenth of the training compute of prior methods at comparable FID, plus text-to-image and world-model results.

frontier.title: Perceptual Flow Matching for Few-Step Generative Modeling
frontier.note: Supervises flow matching in a pretrained perceptual feature space instead of the VAE latent. The authors report 4 to 8 steps instead of 35 to 50 across image, video and editing tasks, with no teacher, arguing the loss becomes mode-seeking rather than mean-seeking.

frontier.title: AnyFlow: Any-Step Video Diffusion Model with On-Policy Flow Map Distillation
frontier.note: Distills video diffusion into flow maps that jump between arbitrary times rather than to the endpoint only. The authors report it matches or beats consistency distillation at few steps and, unlike consistency-distilled models, keeps improving when more steps are allowed (1.3B to 14B models).

frontier.title: One-Step Generative Modeling via Wasserstein Gradient Flows (W-Flow)
frontier.who: Jiaqi Han, Puheng Li et al. (Stanford)
frontier.note: Defines an evolution from noise to data as a Wasserstein gradient flow of the Sinkhorn divergence (an optimal-transport distance), then trains a static generator to compress it into one step. The authors report FID 1.29 on ImageNet 256 and about 100x faster sampling than multi-step models of similar FID.

frontier.title: Generative Modeling via Drifting
frontier.who: Mingyang Deng, He Li, Tianhong Li, Yilun Du, Kaiming He (MIT, Harvard)
frontier.note: Moves the generator's output distribution during training with a drifting field that reaches equilibrium when it matches the data, so sampling is one forward pass. Reports FID 1.54 (latent) and 1.61 (pixel) on ImageNet 256.

frontier.title: One-step Latent-free Image Generation with Pixel Mean Flows
frontier.who: Yiyang Lu et al., Kaiming He (MIT, CMU)
frontier.note: Predicts clean images on the data manifold but applies the MeanFlow loss in velocity space, giving one-step generation directly in pixels: FID 2.22 at 256 and 2.48 at 512 on ImageNet.

frontier.title: Improved Mean Flows: On the Challenges of Fastforward Generative Models
frontier.who: Zhengyang Geng, Yiyang Lu et al., Kaiming He (CMU, MIT, Adobe)
frontier.note: Rewrites the MeanFlow objective as a regression on instantaneous velocity for stability and makes guidance a test-time conditioning input; reports 1-NFE FID 1.72 on ImageNet 256 with no distillation.

frontier.title: Back to Basics: Let Denoising Generative Models Denoise (JiT)
frontier.note: Argues networks should predict clean data, which lies on a low-dimensional manifold, not noise. Plain transformers with 16 and 32 pixel patches on raw pixels, with no tokenizer or pretraining, become competitive on ImageNet.

open: Is the iterative ODE or SDE needed at all, or can one-step objectives like MeanFlow or drifting fully replace multi-step diffusion at scale?
Should generators keep a separate autoencoder, reuse self-supervised encoders, or work in pixels, and how does that change for video?
How do one-step models keep the ability to trade more compute for better samples, and to steer with guidance, editing and reward fine-tuning?
Do ImageNet FID gains transfer to text-to-image and video quality as judged by people, or is the field overfitting a benchmark?

connects.why: The same denoising idea applied to discrete text tokens, generating many tokens in parallel.
Unified models such as Transfusion and BAGEL put a diffusion or flow head inside a language model for image generation.
Robot policies like Diffusion Policy and pi0 generate actions with diffusion and flow matching.
Both are ways to get the output of many sequential model calls for the price of a few.

threads.title: Unified multimodal models, visual tokenizers and video world models
threads.dek: From bolting an image encoder onto a language model, to one network that reads and draws in the same token stream, to models that dream up playable worlds frame by frame.

sections.heading: Two kinds of vision model that want to become one
sections.md:
Until recently, seeing and drawing were separate fields. *Understanding* models take an image and produce text: captions, answers, labels. *Generation* models take text and produce an image, almost always with diffusion. They used different architectures, different training data and different representations of an image.

Language models changed the question. If a transformer can predict the next text token well enough to reason, can the same network also take images in and put images out, in one sequence, with one set of weights? That needs an answer to a hard sub-problem: how to turn an image or a video into something a transformer can read and write. A 512 by 512 image is about 786,000 numbers; a minute of video is orders of magnitude more.

This thread follows three connected questions. How to plug vision into a language model (encoders and adapters). How to tokenize images and video so they can be generated, not just read. And what happens when you push the same idea to video and actions: models of whole interactive worlds.

sections.heading: Reading images: contrastive encoders and adapters
sections.md:
The workhorse came from OpenAI's [CLIP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020) (2021). Train an image encoder and a text encoder so that matching image-caption pairs get similar vectors, using 400 million pairs scraped from the web. The result recognizes concepts it was never explicitly labeled for, just by comparing an image to text prompts. Google's [SigLIP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.15343) (2023) replaced CLIP's batch-wide softmax with an independent sigmoid per pair, which decouples the loss from batch size; SigLIP encoders now sit inside many open vision-language models.

To make a language model see, the simplest move is to feed it the encoder's output. DeepMind's [Flamingo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.14198) (2022) bridged a frozen vision encoder and a frozen language model with new cross-attention layers, trained on web pages with interleaved images and text, and could learn new tasks from a few examples in the prompt. Salesforce's [BLIP-2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.12597) (2023) used a small *Q-Former* that distills a frozen CLIP-family encoder's features into 32 learned query vectors for a frozen LLM. [LLaVA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08485) (Liu et al., 2023) went simpler still: project CLIP features straight into the LLM's input and fine-tune on instruction data that a text-only GPT-4 wrote from image captions.

That *encoder plus projector plus LLM* recipe is how most vision-language models still work. It is excellent at understanding, but it is one-way: continuous encoder features go in, only text comes out.

sections.heading: Writing images: tokenizers, early fusion and hybrids
sections.md:
To generate images with a language model you need discrete image tokens the model can predict, and a decoder that turns them back into pixels. [VQ-VAE](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.00937) (van den Oord et al., DeepMind, 2017) learned exactly that: an autoencoder whose latent is snapped to the nearest entry in a learned codebook. [VQGAN](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.09841) (Esser, Rombach and Ommer, 2020) added adversarial and perceptual losses so codes stay sharp, and modeled their composition with a GPT-style transformer. Google's [MAGVIT-v2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.05737) (2023) argued that the tokenizer is the key component and showed a language model with a good shared image and video tokenizer could beat diffusion on ImageNet and Kinetics benchmarks. [VAR](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.02905) (2024) changed the order of generation from raster scan to coarse-to-fine *next-scale prediction*, improving ImageNet FID (Frechet Inception Distance, lower is better) from 18.65 to 1.73 over its autoregressive baseline.

Meta's [Chameleon](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.09818) (2024) put it together as **early fusion**: every image becomes 1,024 tokens from an 8,192-entry codebook, interleaved with text in one sequence, and one transformer is trained from scratch on both. BAAI's [Emu3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.18869) (2024) pushed the same next-token-only idea to video, with a tokenizer that maps a 512 by 512 image to 4,096 tokens.

Two cracks appeared. Quantization loses detail, and Meta's [Transfusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.11039) (2024) showed that keeping images continuous, training one transformer with a next-token loss on text and a diffusion loss on image patches, scales better than the Chameleon-style discretization. And one visual representation struggles to serve both jobs: DeepSeek's [Janus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13848) (2024) decoupled them, with a SigLIP encoder for understanding and a separate tokenizer for generation, feeding one shared transformer.

sections.heading: From video to worlds: long context and action-conditioned generation
sections.md:
Video multiplies the token problem. [Large World Model](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.08268) (Liu, Yan, Zaharia and Abbeel, Berkeley, 2024) attacked it with brute context: progressively extending a 7B model from 4K to 1M tokens with Blockwise RingAttention so it can read hour-long videos and long documents in one pass.

A different question is whether a model can *simulate* video interactively. DeepMind's [Genie](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.15391) (2024) was trained on 30,000 hours of unlabeled gameplay video from hundreds of 2D platformer games. It has three parts: a spatiotemporal video tokenizer, an autoregressive dynamics model, and a *latent action model* that infers, with a VQ-VAE-style objective, a small discrete set of actions that explain the change between frames. At 11B parameters it lets a user step through a generated world frame by frame without ever seeing true action labels.

[Genie 2](https://deepmind.google/blog/genie-2-a-large-scale-foundation-world-model/) (December 2024) moved to 3D. DeepMind describes it as an autoregressive latent diffusion model: an autoencoder compresses frames and a transformer predicts the next latent frame from past frames and keyboard or mouse actions. From one prompt image it generates worlds that stay consistent for up to a minute and that remember areas that went off screen. DeepMind showed its SIMA agent following language instructions inside Genie 2 worlds.

sections.heading: Where it is now: unified pretraining, world models with memory
sections.md:
**Unified models are scaling up.** ByteDance's [BAGEL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.14683) (May 2025) is an open decoder-only model pretrained on trillions of interleaved text, image, video and web tokens; the authors report emerging abilities such as free-form image editing, future frame prediction and navigation. BAAI's [Emu3.5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.26583) (October 2025) trains next-token prediction on over 10 trillion tokens drawn mainly from video frames and transcripts, then converts token-by-token image decoding into parallel prediction (DiDA), which the authors say speeds image inference about 20 times. 2026 reports such as Shanghai AI Lab's [InternVL-U](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.09877) (4B parameters, a multimodal LLM plus a diffusion generation head) and ByteDance's [Lance](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18678) (dual-stream mixture-of-experts over images and video) converge on one design: shared context, but separate pathways for understanding and generation.

**Long video needs memory, not just context.** Rather than reading every frame at once, methods such as [FlexMem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.29252) (March 2026) treat the visual KV cache (keys and values cached for past frames) as memory, compress what was seen, and recall relevant fragments per question; the authors report over 1,000 frames on a single RTX 3090.

**World models are becoming products.** [Genie 3](https://deepmind.google/blog/genie-3-a-new-frontier-for-world-models/) (August 2025) generates navigable worlds in real time at 720p and 24 fps, consistent for a few minutes with visual memory reaching back about a minute, without any explicit 3D representation; text prompts can trigger world events mid-session. [Genie 4](https://deepmind.google/blog/genie-4-a-new-generation-of-world-simulation/) (October 2026) adds natively generated audio, including character dialogue, and uses Gemini models to guide and check generation; DeepMind says object permanence still drifts over longer sessions. Meta's [V-JEPA 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09985) (June 2025) takes the opposite bet: predict in an abstract representation space instead of pixels, then plan robot actions with it.

lineage.title: Neural Discrete Representation Learning (VQ-VAE)

lineage.contribution: An autoencoder whose latents snap to entries of a learned codebook, giving discrete tokens for images, audio and video that an autoregressive prior can model.

lineage.contribution: Learned a convolutional codebook with adversarial and perceptual losses and generated its tokens with a GPT-style transformer, making token-based high-resolution image generation practical.

lineage.contribution: An 11B world model trained on unlabeled game videos: video tokenizer, autoregressive dynamics model and a latent action model with a VQ-VAE objective, so users can act in generated worlds without action labels.

lineage.contribution: Separate visual pathways (SigLIP features for understanding, a discrete tokenizer for generation) feeding one autoregressive transformer, easing the conflict a single encoder creates.

lineage.title: Genie 2: a large-scale foundation world model
lineage.contribution: Autoregressive latent diffusion world model that turns one prompt image into a playable 3D world, consistent for up to a minute and remembering off-screen areas; tested with SIMA agents.

frontier.title: Genie 4: a new generation of world simulation
frontier.note: Real-time world model that generates audio natively, including ambient sound and character dialogue, with Gemini models guiding and checking generation. A trusted-tester research preview; DeepMind lists long-term consistency and object permanence as unsolved.

frontier.title: Introducing Gemini Omni
frontier.note: First model of an any-to-any family, Gemini Omni Flash, takes text, images, video and voice audio as input and outputs video, with conversational multi-turn editing that keeps scenes consistent. Google says image and audio output will follow; architecture details are not published. The Genie 4 post says Gemini Omni anchors its simulations.

frontier.title: Lance: Unified Multimodal Modeling by Multi-Task Synergy
frontier.note: A lightweight model trained from scratch for understanding, generation and editing of both images and video, using a dual-stream mixture-of-experts so the tasks share context but keep separate pathways.

frontier.title: Scaling the Long Video Understanding of Multimodal LLMs via Visual Memory Mechanism (FlexMem)
frontier.note: Training-free: treats visual KV caches as memory, compresses them as the video streams, and recalls relevant fragments per question. The authors report handling over 1,000 frames on one RTX 3090 across five long-video and one streaming task.

frontier.title: Emu3.5: Native Multimodal Models are World Learners
frontier.note: Next-token pretraining on over 10 trillion interleaved tokens, mostly video frames and transcripts, plus RL post-training. Converts sequential image decoding to parallel prediction for about 20 times faster image inference, per the authors.

frontier.title: Genie 3: a new frontier for world models
frontier.note: Real-time interactive worlds at 720p and 24 fps, consistent for a few minutes with roughly one minute of visual memory, with no explicit 3D representation. Text prompts can change weather or add objects mid-session.

frontier.title: V-JEPA 2: Self-Supervised Video Models Enable Understanding, Prediction and Planning
frontier.note: Predicts in representation space rather than pixels. Pretrained on over 1 million hours of video, then an action-conditioned version trained on under 62 hours of robot video plans pick-and-place zero-shot on Franka arms.

frontier.title: BAGEL: Emerging Properties in Unified Multimodal Pretraining
frontier.note: Open decoder-only unified model pretrained on trillions of interleaved text, image, video and web tokens; the authors report abilities such as free-form editing and future frame prediction emerging with scale.

open: Should one visual representation serve both understanding and generation, or is a decoupled design fundamentally better?
Discrete tokens or continuous latents for images and video inside a language model: which scales better when compute is matched?
How can video world models keep objects and places consistent for hours rather than minutes without an explicit 3D map?
Can long-video models remember selectively, like a person, instead of reading or caching every frame?
Do world models trained on video learn usable physics and causality, or mainly plausible appearance?

connects.why: Diffusion and flow heads generate the pixels inside hybrid models like Transfusion and world models like Genie 2.
Visual tokenizers face the same compression versus fidelity trade-off as text tokenizers.
VLAs are VLMs extended with actions, and world models like V-JEPA 2 and Genie are used to train or plan for robots.
CLIP-style encoders power image search, and ColPali retrieves documents by embedding page images.
Million-token video contexts depend on ring and blockwise attention and on KV cache compression.

threads.title: Robots and 3D: vision-language-action models and Gaussian splatting
threads.dek: Two ways AI is leaving the screen: robot policies built on top of vision-language models, and 3D scenes captured from photos and rendered in real time as millions of soft colored blobs.

sections.heading: Acting in the physical world, and seeing it in 3D
sections.md:
Language models learned from the whole internet. Robots have nothing comparable: every demonstration of a robot folding a shirt has to be collected by a person teleoperating a real machine, one episode at a time. Classic robot learning therefore trained a separate small policy for each task, each robot and often each room, and those policies broke when anything changed.

The bet behind **vision-language-action models (VLAs)** is to borrow the internet anyway. Start from a vision-language model that already knows what a mug, a drawer and "the smallest object" are, and teach it to output motor commands as well as words. The open questions are how to represent actions, how to pool data across very different robots, and how to make the result fast and precise enough for real hands.

The second half of this thread is about representing the world those robots move through. Given photos of a scene, *novel view synthesis* renders it from new viewpoints. Neural radiance fields (NeRF) made this photorealistic in 2020 but were slow to train and render. 3D Gaussian splatting replaced the neural network with millions of explicit 3D blobs and made it real-time, and it has since become a file format, a capture product and a building block for simulation.

sections.heading: From NeRF to Gaussian splatting
sections.md:
[NeRF](https://arxiv.org/abs/2003.08934) (Mildenhall et al., UC Berkeley and Google, 2020) represents a scene as a neural network: given a 3D point and viewing direction, it returns density and color. An image is rendered by marching along each camera ray, querying the network at many points and blending the results (*volume rendering*). Because that is differentiable, the network can be fit to posed photos with plain gradient descent. Quality was striking, but every pixel needs many network calls.

Two 2021 to 2022 papers showed the big network was the bottleneck. [Plenoxels](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.05131) (UC Berkeley) dropped neural networks entirely for a sparse voxel grid with spherical harmonics colors and optimized two orders of magnitude faster than NeRF. NVIDIA's [Instant-NGP](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.05989) kept a tiny network but fed it features from a multiresolution hash table, training in seconds.

[3D Gaussian Splatting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04079) (Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkuhler and Drettakis, Inria, 2023) took the explicit route further. The scene is a cloud of 3D Gaussians, each with a position, an anisotropic covariance (an oriented ellipsoid), an opacity and view-dependent color. They start from the sparse points that camera calibration already produces, and optimization moves, splits, clones and prunes them. Rendering projects each Gaussian to the screen and alpha-blends them in depth order with a fast tile-based rasterizer, with no ray marching. The paper reports real-time (at least 30 fps) rendering at 1080p, and its headline example reaches state-of-the-art quality after 51 minutes of training (about 6 minutes gives quality similar to Instant-NGP).

Follow-ups fixed the representation's weak spots. [Mip-Splatting](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.16493) (Tubingen, 2023) removed aliasing when zooming by limiting Gaussian size to the input sampling frequency. NVIDIA's [3DGUT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.12507) (2024) replaced the splatting projection with an unscented transform so fisheye lenses, rolling shutter and secondary rays (reflections) work, which matters for robotics and driving sensors.

sections.heading: From robot transformers to vision-language-action models
sections.md:
Google's [RT-1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.06817) (2022) showed a single transformer trained on a large, diverse real-robot dataset generalizes better as data, model size and diversity grow. [RT-2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15818) (2023) made the key move: take a large vision-language model, write the robot's actions as text tokens (discretized as in RT-1), and co-fine-tune on robot trajectories and web vision-language data together. The paper named the result a **vision-language-action model** and reported, over 6,000 trials, emergent skills absent from the robot data, such as placing an object on a particular number or picking an improvised hammer.

Data was the next bottleneck. [Open X-Embodiment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.08864) (2023) pooled data from 22 robot types across 21 institutions and showed RT-X models trained on the mix transfer positively across robots. [Octo](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.12213) (2024) and [OpenVLA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09246) (2024) made generalist policies open. OpenVLA, a 7B model built on Llama 2 with DINOv2 and SigLIP vision features and trained on 970k demonstrations, reports 16.5 points higher task success than the 55B RT-2-X.

Text tokens are a poor fit for fast, smooth motion. [Diffusion Policy](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.04137) (Columbia and Toyota Research, 2023) instead generated chunks of continuous actions by denoising, reporting a 46.9% average improvement across 12 tasks. Physical Intelligence's [pi0](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.24164) (2024) combined both lines: a PaliGemma VLM plus a smaller *action expert* that outputs action chunks by flow matching (a diffusion-like generator), controlling robots at up to 50 Hz, pretrained on about 10,000 hours of its own data plus Open X-Embodiment. [FAST](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.09747) (January 2025) compressed action chunks with a discrete cosine transform into efficient tokens, matching diffusion VLAs with up to 5 times less training. [pi0.5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.16054) (April 2025) trains on FAST tokens and decodes with flow matching, and co-trains on web data and high-level subtask prediction to clean kitchens and bedrooms in homes it never saw.

sections.heading: Where it is now: learning from experience, steerable policies, feed-forward 3D
sections.md:
**Robots that improve from their own attempts.** Imitation alone copies the demonstrator's mistakes and cannot exceed them. Physical Intelligence's [pi*0.6](https://www.pi.website/blog/pistar06) (November 2025) adds Recap: a learned value function scores how each action changed the odds of success, and the policy is conditioned on that *advantage* and asked for high-advantage actions, mixing in teleoperator corrections. The company reports more than double the throughput on some of its hardest tasks and failure rates cut by 2 times or more. DeepMind's [Gemini Robotics 1.5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.03342) (October 2025) has the VLA interleave natural-language reasoning with actions ("think before acting") and adds Motion Transfer to learn across different robot bodies. DeepMind says its successor, [Gemini Robotics 2](https://deepmind.google/models/gemini-robotics/) (July 2026), controls whole humanoid bodies.

**Steerable generalists.** [pi0.7](https://www.pi.website/blog/pi07) (April 2026) is trained with prompts that describe not only the task but how to do it: episode metadata such as speed and quality, control mode, and subgoal images produced by a small world model. Annotating quality lets it learn from imperfect autonomous data. The company reports it matching its RL-trained pi*0.6 specialists on laundry, espresso and box building, and early compositional generalization; these are developer-run lab results.

**3D without per-scene optimization.** [AnySplat](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.23716) (May 2025) predicts Gaussians and camera poses for uncalibrated photo collections in one forward pass. [StreamSplat](https://arxiv.org/abs/2608.01659) (August 2026) updates a scene causally as views stream in, with memory that grows with explored geometry rather than stream length, which is what a moving robot needs. And splats are becoming infrastructure: in September 2026 Khronos [ratified KHR_gaussian_splatting](https://github.com/KhronosGroup/glTF/tree/main/extensions/2.0/Khronos/KHR_gaussian_splatting), after a February release candidate, a standard way to store splats in glTF 2.0.

lineage.title: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis
lineage.who: Ben Mildenhall et al. (UC Berkeley, Google Research, UC San Diego)
lineage.contribution: A network maps 3D position and view direction to density and color; differentiable volume rendering fits it to posed photos, giving photorealistic novel views at high compute cost.

lineage.title: Plenoxels: Radiance Fields without Neural Networks
lineage.who: Alex Yu, Sara Fridovich-Keil et al. (UC Berkeley)
lineage.contribution: Replaced the network with a sparse voxel grid of densities and spherical harmonics, optimizing two orders of magnitude faster than NeRF at similar quality.

lineage.title: Instant Neural Graphics Primitives with a Multiresolution Hash Encoding
lineage.who: Thomas Muller, Alex Evans, Christoph Schied, Alexander Keller (NVIDIA)
lineage.contribution: A tiny MLP fed by a trainable multiresolution hash table, implemented in fused CUDA kernels, cutting radiance field training to seconds.

lineage.title: RT-1: Robotics Transformer for Real-World Control at Scale
lineage.contribution: One transformer policy trained on a large, diverse real-robot dataset, studying how generalization scales with data size, model size and diversity; defined the discretized action format RT-2 reused.

lineage.title: Diffusion Policy: Visuomotor Policy Learning via Action Diffusion
lineage.who: Cheng Chi et al. (Columbia, Toyota Research Institute)
lineage.contribution: Generates chunks of continuous actions by denoising, handling multimodal action distributions; reported a 46.9% average improvement over prior methods across 12 tasks.

lineage.title: RT-2: Vision-Language-Action Models Transfer Web Knowledge to Robotic Control
lineage.contribution: Wrote robot actions as text tokens and co-fine-tuned large VLMs on robot and web data, naming the VLA category and showing emergent semantic skills over 6,000 trials.

lineage.title: 3D Gaussian Splatting for Real-Time Radiance Field Rendering
lineage.who: Kerbl, Kopanas, Leimkuhler, Drettakis (Inria, MPI Informatik)
lineage.contribution: Explicit scenes of anisotropic 3D Gaussians optimized with adaptive densification and drawn by a tile-based rasterizer: real-time 1080p novel views at state-of-the-art quality.

lineage.title: Open X-Embodiment: Robotic Learning Datasets and RT-X Models
lineage.contribution: Pooled data from 22 robot types and 527 skills in a standard format; RT-X models trained on the mix showed positive transfer across robots.

lineage.title: Mip-Splatting: Alias-free 3D Gaussian Splatting
lineage.who: Zehao Yu et al. (University of Tubingen)
lineage.contribution: A 3D smoothing filter tied to input sampling frequency and a 2D Mip filter remove the aliasing and dilation artifacts 3DGS shows when zooming or changing resolution.

lineage.title: Octo: An Open-Source Generalist Robot Policy
lineage.who: Octo Model Team (Dibya Ghosh, Homer Walke et al.)
lineage.contribution: Open transformer policy trained on 800k Open X-Embodiment trajectories, steerable by language or goal images and fine-tunable to new robots in hours on consumer GPUs.

lineage.title: OpenVLA: An Open-Source Vision-Language-Action Model
lineage.who: Moo Jin Kim, Karl Pertsch et al. (Stanford, UC Berkeley, TRI, Google DeepMind)
lineage.contribution: Open 7B VLA (Llama 2 with DINOv2 and SigLIP features) trained on 970k demonstrations; 16.5 points higher success than the 55B RT-2-X, with efficient fine-tuning recipes.

lineage.title: pi0: A Vision-Language-Action Flow Model for General Robot Control
lineage.contribution: A PaliGemma VLM plus an action expert that outputs continuous action chunks by flow matching at up to 50 Hz, pretrained on about 10,000 hours of robot data plus Open X-Embodiment.

lineage.title: 3DGUT: Enabling Distorted Cameras and Secondary Rays in Gaussian Splatting
lineage.contribution: Replaces EWA splatting with an unscented transform so Gaussians project exactly under any camera model, supporting fisheye, rolling shutter, reflections and refractions while staying rasterized.

lineage.title: FAST: Efficient Action Tokenization for Vision-Language-Action Models
lineage.contribution: Compresses action chunks with a discrete cosine transform into compact tokens; autoregressive pi0-FAST matches diffusion VLAs while training up to 5 times faster.

lineage.title: pi0.5: a Vision-Language-Action Model with Open-World Generalization
lineage.contribution: Co-trains on multi-robot data, web data and high-level subtask prediction, using FAST tokens in pretraining and flow matching for actions, to do long-horizon cleaning in unseen homes.

frontier.title: Khronos ratifies the KHR_gaussian_splatting glTF extension
frontier.who: The Khronos Group (Cesium, Niantic Spatial, Esri, NVIDIA and others)
frontier.note: After a release candidate in February 2026, the baseline extension for storing 3D Gaussian splats (position, rotation, scale, opacity, spherical harmonics) as glTF 2.0 point primitives was marked Complete, Ratified in September 2026; a step from research artifact to interchange format.

frontier.title: StreamSplat: Streaming Feed-Forward 3D Gaussian Splatting
frontier.note: Builds a 3D Gaussian scene causally as calibrated views arrive, using a voxel-aligned cache whose memory grows with explored geometry rather than stream length; competitive with offline feed-forward methods without seeing future views.

frontier.title: Gemini Robotics 2, Gemini Robotics ER 2 and Gemini Robotics On-Device 2
frontier.note: The next generation of DeepMind's VLA family. The company says Gemini Robotics 2 controls whole humanoid bodies from feet to fingertips, adapts to a new bi-arm robot in a few hours and coordinates several robots, with ER 2 doing planning. These are company claims from the launch page, not independent evaluations.

frontier.title: pi0.7: a steerable generalist robot model
frontier.note: Trained with prompts that specify how to act (speed and quality metadata, control mode, subgoal images from a small world model), letting it learn from imperfect autonomous data. The company reports matching its RL-trained specialists on several tasks.

frontier.title: pi*0.6 and Recap: a VLA that learns from experience
frontier.note: Trains a value function, conditions the policy on the advantage of each action, and mixes in teleoperator corrections. Reports over 2 times throughput on some hard tasks and failure rates cut by 2 times or more, such as making espresso through a full day.

frontier.title: Gemini Robotics 1.5
frontier.note: A multi-embodiment VLA that interleaves natural-language reasoning with actions, a Motion Transfer mechanism to learn from different robots, and an embodied-reasoning model for planning and progress estimation.

frontier.title: AnySplat: Feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting from Unconstrained Views
frontier.who: Lihan Jiang et al. (USTC, Shanghai AI Laboratory)
frontier.note: One forward pass turns an uncalibrated photo collection into Gaussians plus camera intrinsics and extrinsics, matching pose-aware baselines in zero-shot tests and removing per-scene optimization.

open: Where will robot data at internet scale come from: teleoperation fleets, autonomous practice, human video, or simulation and world models?
Is a single VLA across many robot bodies better than specialists once enough data exists, and how should actions be represented?
How can robot policies be evaluated reproducibly when every lab reports success rates on its own hardware and tasks?
Can splat scenes carry physics, semantics and editability well enough to serve as robot simulators, not just pretty renders?
Will feed-forward 3D reconstruction match per-scene optimized quality for large, dynamic scenes?

connects.why: VLAs are vision-language models extended with actions, and video world models (Genie, V-JEPA 2) are used to plan and train robots.
Diffusion Policy and pi0's action expert generate actions with diffusion and flow matching.
Recap brings advantage-conditioned RL from experience to VLAs, echoing RL post-training of language models.
Embodied reasoning models plan and call tools for a low-level policy, like software agents orchestrating actions.
